item.title: AI is forcing us to pay off 40 years of technical debt
item.description: 932 points, 570 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (spectrum.ieee.org)

→ HN comments  ·  932 points  ·  570 comments

Top #1 — Balgair:

Aside: I think I need some help here.[0]

I remember reading Godel Escher Bach back in the day, and there is the parable of the record player between the tortoise and the rabbit. And the tortoise keeps building more and more secure record players that the rabbit keeps finding ways to break.

GEB then goes on to teach you that, no, in fact, you cannot have a perfectly secure system. Not just practically or economically, but even in theory, all systems are fundamentally breakable. GEB, after a lot of chapters (what a doorstop!) ties that parable into Godel's Incompleteness Theorem, and essentially proves that no, you can't make unbreakable things, as a fundamental point of logic.

So, when I look at all this, I see that yes, there is an economics point of view here, that fixing code is just expensive, like making a less and less breakable record player. And that AIs push that breaking and economics point much further along than what we have had.

But then I also see a lot of comments here that seem (to me) to be arguing that there is an unbreakable code out there.

Am I reading this right? Is there such a thing as 'perfect' code? Or is my outdated reading of GEB still valid or not?

[0]Note, I'm not a CS person, more a biophysics person.

↳ reply — zeroonetwothree:

A specific system could be proven to be secure. There is no general mechanism to prove all software secure however.

Top #2 — Arbortheus:

I hope some of these backdoors and/or 0-days being kept under wraps by nation states or corporate espionage companies (Pegasus et al) are being found incidentally through all this.

It’s frustrating to have all these 0days and CVEs to patch for now, but in the long run perhaps we’ll leave with more robust software.

↳ reply 1 — Loquebantur:

The logical extrapolation of AI capabilities stress-testing human software is all bugs being discoverable. Hence, you have to aim for actually bug-free software.

The only way to do that is to make your code provable. That again is only realistically doable using AI.

In the process, people will have to turn the pretense of "software engineering" into reality, making the engineering part explicit.

That only works when humans actually understand what they're doing.

↳↳ reply — dbingham:

While I whole-heartedly support the goal of actually bug free software and treating software engineering as a serious engineering discipline, as an experienced software engineer who also studied physics, I have to challenge your base premise about what it means to make engineering explicit.

Namely:

> The only way to do that is to make your code provable.

Proofs are a mathematical concept. They only work in the abstract world of mathematics where everything is perfectly logical.

Engineering exists in the real world. The physical realm where our mathematics are only imperfect models of what actually exists. Removing bugs through physical engineering requires persistent trial and error until you have found all the places where our mathematical models don't adequately represent the real world.

It's the same in software engineering, which involves cobbling together a myriad of systems not all designed to talk to each other and massive, ever changing codebases where perfect knowledge is impossible.

So yes, we should be trying to engineer bug free code. But that's really more a matter of changing our resource allocation, spending more time and money on QA and doing away with mottos like "Move fast and break things". It's a cultural shift and will only come when the bosses -- the venture capitalists who ultimately control our industry -- are held accountable when things break, and given strong incentives to ensure they don't break.

↳↳↳ reply — Loquebantur:

The physical world is actually part of mathematics. Look into John Archibald Wheeler and his "It from bit". In particular, the physical world is finite. Therefore, mathematical proofs very much apply to physics.

You're right about approximations: we gather data and improve theoretical models in an attempt to exhaust that complexity reality poses.

You're wrong about exhaustive knowledge about codebases being impossible. LLMs enable exactly that.

The trick then is to transfer that knowledge in a usable way to what we know about the codebase.

I agree with the necessary cultural shift.

↳ reply 2 — ChuckMcM:

As a testing tool, yes, post AI software is going to be more robust in the face of attack. We saw this when Metasploit became a thing, it provided an easy way for web site owners to test their stack against 'known problems.' I think that as a rule, we won't get a lot of action on this until we change the laws around incidental damages liability with regards to software.

It is also unfortunate than in more than half the cases where AI provides a 'fix' that fix breaks something else, so my guess is this is going to be 90% human labor to correct, at least initially.

Top #3 — swatcoder:

Is it forcing us to "pay off" technical debt or is it starting us on a compulsory endless treadmill of feature-neutral fix-work? Collectively, we just won't know for a while.

It totally feels like the former if you watch it find and fix vulnerabilities or other debt-tasks one after another.

But only so many of these "technical debt" issue are little off-by-one errors that get remedied by a surgically narrow patch.

Many enough require some kind of restructuring or redevelopment of their own and it's going to take time to figure out if AI faces the same dilemma as human developers: where each non-trivial change carries the risk of some new issue, ad infinitum.

If that happens to be the case, and AI isn't able to magically produce perfect software in finite time, then what's really happened is that the threat of hostile AI exploiting our technical debt will force us to always be burning and churning code just to remain a moving target.

It's another "we'll see" thing for now, I think.

↳ reply 1 — intrasight:

The original technical debt, which cannot be paid off, was the decision to use a Von Neumann architectures instead of a Harvard architectures for CPUs.

↳↳ reply — victorbjorklund:

Explain? (Genuine question because I wanna know)

↳↳↳ reply — GTP:

Basically, have an explicit distinction between data and code at the architectural level, to enforce "Write xor Execute" in hardware. In this way, you would prevent e.g. a buffer overflow letting an attacker injecting shellcode that gets executed later by somehow pointing at it. AFAIK the issue would still remain with some programming languages though.

↳ reply 2 — hashmap:

the equilibrium state would be having found a good pattern for making patterns good. we probably aren't too far from that, so i think your worry may show up in the short term but not the long one

Top #1 — nerdjon:

This is frustrating, I have had a growing distrust (and just frustration with the software in the first place) of DisplayLink with the Dock that I use, I would love alternative software.

This also just seems stupid to me, you don't pay for the DisplayLink software you pay for the hardware. More options for how to use your hardware would be a good thing to them would it not?

That's the problem when you have lawyers in charge. To a lawyer, Drivers and Hardware are the same thing: IP. That IP needs to be "protected", period, end of story.

The developer of the driver is in the UK. Given how the UK legal system works, I understand why the developer likely sees non-compliance with Synaptics’ demands as involving excessive personal risk.

I mentioned Europe in an other comment, as software is mostly not patentable there. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_patents_under_the_Eur...>

Top #3 — nijave:

If they were smart, they'd welcome an effort to make DisplayLink not a piece of trash.

↳ reply — bdavbdav:

item.title: Geoffrey Hinton: it might turn out we were better off without AI
item.description: 291 points, 287 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (theguardian.com)

→ HN comments  ·  291 points  ·  287 comments

Top #1 — mrweasel:

If the people in charge of the AI companies understand the risk I don't know, but I think it's a good point that they mainly care about the money. These are also people who aren't accustom to cleaning up their own mess, so what do they care if something goes wrong.

The carelessness is also clear in how AI is rolled out. It's being presented as a disruptive technology, as is everything else presented by modern tech companies. The goal is a very large payout in a very short period of time, it's not to make anything better, or worse, either is just a side effect.

Had LLMs first been presented as a "better IntelliSense", where rather than auto-completing function names, your editor can now suggest implementations, very few people would have been upset. Same for writing, it's just a better version of Grammarly, it's fine, or as a tool in drawing software. The issue would have been, for the AI bosses, that this takes time and doesn't create trillion dollar companies. It only creates companies that they'd actually have to run, long term, and that's boring.

↳ reply 1 — Aurornis:

> The issue would have been, for the AI bosses, that this takes time and doesn't create trillion dollar companies. It only creates companies that they'd actually have to run, long term, and that's boring.

I feel like you’re not acknowledging the inevitability of the technology being developed further. You’re also ignoring competition and the basic fact that people do research and push the boundaries of their field naturally.

If the major frontier AI labs had decided, as you said, to make a fancy autocomplete and a better Grammarly and then simply stop and coast, do you really believe that every AI researcher and entrepreneur in the entire world would look at the situation and decide that the status quo is where it should end?

Humans don’t work that way. People would get ideas and want to push the limit. If the frontier labs stopped developing their technology, other companies would be created to carry on. Academic researchers would push the limits further. It would be discovered that the AI could go further and we’d get back to this same eventuality with a different set of people leading it.

I also disagree with your characterization of this as a get rich quick scheme for AI leaders who want to make a lot of money and then be done. I think this characterization feels truthy if your only conception of startups is as a gamble to retire early, but the people who build and run these companies actually do like building and running companies. If the AI leaders and executive management you’re talking about were separated from their jobs today, even with billions of equity, most of them would be out starting new companies next month because that’s what people like that do. I’m not saying this to “glaze” them or whatever I’ll surely be accused of in the comments, I’m stating some facts about this space. You don’t need to look far to find examples of this already happening.

↳↳ reply — rafterydj:

I really don't like the excuses that are inherent to the "well it was inevitable" line of thinking. Oppenheimer was still responsible for the bomb despite it being "inevitable" in a similar way.

Despite this, when discussing the egregious behavior of the frontier labs, there is vanishingly little acceptance of the idea that 1) yes, it probably was inevitable in some ways AND 2) those involved, particularly at the top, are still responsible for the consequences of their (bad) decisions.

↳↳↳ reply — mcv:

Both nuclear bombs and AI are not inevitable. Technology depends not just on knowledge, but on infrastructure. Building and maintaining nuclear bombs requires enormous amounts of resources, and it's a conscious decision to continue spending those resources to maintain nuclear capability. Similarly, developing AI requires enormous resources, as you can see from the massive investments in hardware and data centers. If the economic foundation for it doesn't exist, you're not going to get more powerful AI.

The models we currently have aren't going away, and especially the ones small enough to run at home will continue to be used, but if these data center investments end up bankrupting Big Tech, I don't think we're ever going to see anything beyond that. Not for a long time, at least.

↳ reply 2 — Telemakhos:

AI has an extremely high capital barrier to research and development. Getting that initial capital required promises of a world-changing technology. A few companies with lots of investment were able to develop the technology and roll their own models. The business case for this R&D was that providing the models to paying users would amortize the R&D costs. But, promising disruption was the first step to getting the money.

Then the Chinese came along and showed that you can take those model weights, repackage them as open weights, and undercut the business model. Suddenly Dario et al. start talking about how dangerous AI is and how it needs to be regulated right now, before someone's abliterated open-weight Chinese-provided business-undercutting model destroys the world. They want their walled gardens regulated into being the only game available.

Both stages of the game—raising capital and regulatory capture—require hyping up the disruptive aspect of AI.

↳ reply 3 — roenxi:

There are a huge number of people involved in AI outside of the major AI companies both in smaller AI companies and lots of independent developers. They aren't having much success bringing AI to the masses and this is because they don't care enough about money and they aren't selling their ideas aggressively enough. There is this odd tendency to undersell achievements because they weren't motivated by the Right Stuff.

The AI companies are as much being pushed along by investors as they are in the driving seat, but the push is in the direction of getting real products in front of people and experimenting with this miraculous tech everywhere it could possible work.

Top #2 — bvan:

Of course, we are. Back in the late 80’s early 90’s, no one working on ML was aspiring to develop systems which would be used to generate the kind of AI crap which plagues us today.The good is being smothered by the absolutely soul-crushing pointless.

↳ reply 1 — lagrange77:

I hear you and i find it devastating, too. On top of that, the negative effects on the planet for having this technology vomit this soul-crushingly pointless crap is just depressing.

↳ reply 2 — kajumix:

AI exposes the Sturgeon's law (90% of everything is crap), and amplifies it much more, and anything good is drowned out. Most of human-generated popular music is slop. Most of human generated code is buggy, unmaintainable and full of debt. Social media and youtube have always been dominated by click-bait and mediocre time-wasting crap.

Top #3 — rickydroll:

My life was not better without AI. It's my accessibility tool. Speech recognition is far better than anything Dragon produced (I use Aqua). And I can now write code again. It's been 30 years since I've been able to do anything significant without pain. It is incredibly liberating to be able to finally write what's in my head and make the code function.

Having AI in my life is a hill I will die on. I will not want to go back to being dependent on having other people do for me what AI lets me do for myself.

↳ reply — reasonableklout:

Ok, but Hinton is worried about what happens if the tech keeps getting better at the current pace.

Let's flip your last point: if the tech gets good enough to replace people at any task (including physical ones), do you think others will need you for much?

And then there's the systems that the corporations are making more powerful as fast as they can. Yes, they promise to do things like cure cancer, but they're also capable of scarier things like hacking banks. And they're progressing faster than we can understand them. Would it be so bad to delay the cancer cures by a couple years to ensure we still understand what the models are doing?

↳↳ reply — rickydroll:

I don't care if others need me, and here's why.

With AI-driven speech recognition, I have far more agency than I did without, period. I can write, I can code, I can communicate with various entities, people, government organizations, corporations, chatbots. I can fill in online forms instead of leaving a bunch of spastic scrawls that generate more questions. I can use it to drive OpenSCAD and 3d print something.

And here's why I start out by saying I don't care if others need me.

I think I'm congenitally incapable of not building/designing/exploring things. If we had an AI-dominated future and we were all on UBI, I'd still find myself saying “hmmm, I wonder” and going down a rat hole to see what I can find. I'm doing it for myself. My curiosity and satisfaction in bringing something to life, even if it's only a variation on what somebody else did.

Rephrasing something I said in a comment somewhere that I would spend time gardening, bird watching, and building a closer relationship with my partner and my pets. I would have no want of things to do or explore.

To your last point, we don't need to understand how something works for it to be useful. Doctors don't understand why treatments work and why they fail. If doctors waited, if treatments waited until they understood how and why it worked, I'd probably be dead. But because they don't, I now have a VP shunt in my head (aka, medical-grade juice-box straw), and my life has drastically improved. Toddlers are something parents don't understand—the how or why they do what they do—but they keep having them anyway.

WTF moments are an emergent property of toddlers, goats, border collies, working dogs, hunting dogs, and AI agents. And like with a toddler, we need to deal with it like we're the adults in the room.

Too many people in my life have died of cancer, and the agony and pain as their body hollows out to a waxen shell is something I'll probably never forget. If I had a choice between understanding how AI works and a cancer cure, I would choose the cancer cure, hands down.

One thing we do need to do is slow down the development or the build-out of AI data centers and put a resource constraint on the model companies, forcing them to get better with the same resources. Sort of an economic “you can't have dessert until you've eaten your vegetables” moment.

I really got to sit down and write that blog post on why agents are like toddlers and that toddlers should have figurative machine guns.

item.title: Tell HN: Gemini trains on chat history, even for subscribers (personal accounts)
item.description: 560 points, 145 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article

→ HN comments  ·  560 points  ·  145 comments

Top #1 — fny:

"These chat transcripts may even be read by human reviewers."

PSA: This is true of all the frontier model providers even if you disable activity tracking. They are all constantly monitoring your interactions for problematic behavior.

[0]: https://www.nytimes.com/wirecutter/advice/ai-chat-privacy/

[1]: https://www.404media.co/inside-project-lily-the-humans-readi...

[2]: https://www.winknews.com/news/woman-arrested-after-ai-threat...

↳ reply 1 — gkcnlr:

The sole reason LLMs has gotten this good is because their aggressive expansion has been accompanied with literally this. The amount of uncredited information these models have been fed must be astonishing, also terrifying.

↳↳ reply — synalx:

I think the heavily subsidized subscriptions are exactly for this purpose - the training data they generate is worth the high subsidy.

↳↳↳ reply — red-iron-pine:

i mean openai basically said as much, no? it's free for all so that they can train the models better and get real world interaction data.

↳ reply 2 — cududa:

That is, fundamentally the marketing ploy of “AI Safety”.

For an AI system to be “completely safe”, like a self-driving car, it must map the full environment it operates in and be taught the “right way” to handle every conceivable scenario.

So when you present it with novel data or a situation, that constitutes an “AI safety event”, which per their ToS is a carve out for training on your session.

Further, go read the ToS carefully about what you opt out of. You’ll note there’s nary a mention of tool calls. You’re only opting out inputs (what you type) and outputs from the model from being trained on. All the content of the tool calls made while running on your system are fair game for training.

↳ reply 3 — fierycatnet:

I can guarantee you that multiple people are reviewing some chats. This is very similar to Apen and whatever company prior to that for reviewing Google searches. They'd hire out contractors with NDA.

Top #2 — richrichardsson:

What's worse is if you have a Pixel phone then Gemini is completely useless without enabling this setting.

I had it switched off:

"Hey Google, remind me at 7pm <something>"

"OK, your reminder is set for 7pm"

Next day:

"Hey Google, why didn't you remind me at 7pm"

"I can't do anything with your phone unless you enable chat history."

WTAF!

↳ reply 1 — devsda:

This was the case with Google Assistant too.

Google has this pattern of all or nothing approach.

Maps refuses to show your *current* location if you don't enable location accuracy i.e. if you won't allow it to spy on your WiFi or Bluetooth it refuses to show your current location at all. GPS, what's that?

We can disable notifications and even phone access but physical activity is the one permission that cannot be disabled for play services !?

Google apps have a lot of WTFs!

↳↳ reply — BoppreH:

And the YouTube home page is blank if you have Watch History off. The recommendation algorithm still runs on the side bar of any video you watch, but the home page refuses to even show your subscriptions.

↳↳↳ reply — SoftTalker:

That could be seen as a feature.

↳ reply 2 — rhema:

Worst part is that the history lives with your other gemini chats. So, "set timer for x" 85 times gets muddled into chats where I'm doing deep research.

Top #3 — devsda:

> Please don’t enter confidential information that you wouldn’t want a reviewer to see or Google

If Gemini has access to app data like gallery, mail etc that can also be subjected to human review? I imagine that will also be part of the context.

They are vague when they say 'don't enter'. Is it only prompts or does it also cover other data too.

↳ reply 1 — hanspeter:

Your email, Google docs, Google photos, Google home devices etc. are all subject to human review. The data is on their servers.

And this goes for all cloud providers btw.

↳ reply 2 — illwrks:

Exactly, I have a Gemini Pro account, I can’t see how privacy can be maintained. If I ask Gemini to take the content of an email and added the dates to my calendar, then all of that private information might as well be public then!

item.title: Verification Is Not Knowledge: Science needs more than answers
item.description: 204 points, 121 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (blog.cosmos-institute.org)

→ HN comments  ·  204 points  ·  121 comments

Top #1 — throw0101c:

When Kepler published his models:

* https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler%27s_laws_of_planetary_m...

People did not understand how or why they worked, but they switched over to them from the Ptolemaic (Tychonic, etc†) system anyway because the math was easier. It was only later (Newton, Einstein) that we understood the "why" and "how".

† https://tofspot.blogspot.com/2013/08/the-great-ptolemaic-sma...

↳ reply 1 — advisedwang:

Kepler did understand the data he had, where it came from, what his laws were claiming, how to verify that the data fits the laws, how the data dis-proves heliocentricity etc, which is really what the article is talking about.

↳↳ reply — throw0101c:

Kepler's models showed that the planets travelling in elliptical orbits matched observations, but Ptolemy (and Brahe, etc) also produced models that (tried to) match observation.

If Kepler's models explained the how and why, why were Newton and Einstein necessary?

↳↳↳ reply — dfabulich:

Newton and Einstein answered "how" questions with more generality and more precision.

Kepler's model predicted the behavior of the planets, and so does Newton's model, but Newton's model is more general, applying not only to planets, but also to apples, cannonballs, trains, and other objects with mass.

Einstein's model is more accurate and precise than Newton's model, especially about the orbit of Mercury. Einstein's model also predicts gravitational lensing (e.g. during eclipses), which Newton's model doesn't.

"Why" questions are very hard for physicists. Generally, when we ask "why" questions, we're asking what prior Event X caused Event Y. But for universal laws, there is no prior event that caused the universal law to be true. The best we get is more generality. Planets orbit the sun for the same reason apples fall to the earth, but we don't know why gravity happens, only how. Magnets resist each other for the same reason the floor is hard, but we don't know why magnetism happens, only how.

↳ reply 2 — godelski:

I'd be careful with the inference you're making here. Tbh we could easily conclude that neither Newton nor Einstein explained "why". One could argue we still don't know and won't even after we have a TOE.

I'd take Asimov's "Relativity of Wrong" here. And I also think there's motivation for why scientists care so much about elegance.

↳ reply 3 — MillironX:

When the article brought up the cancer drug analogy, I thought roughly the same thing. We still don't know why certain drugs work (take gabapentin as a prime example), but we're still comfortable using them on a regular basis.

Top #2 — niemandhier:

We all know Terry Tao, do you know Peter Scholz?

Fields medalist and as Tao listed as one of the most important mathematicians of our age.

Scholz is known to find „precisely the correct and cleanest way to incorporate all the previously done work and find an elegant formulation for that — and then, because he found really the correct framework, go way beyond the known results“

In a way that man is the complement of an AI, he generates understanding rather than just proofs.

Maybe he is the right template for the mathematicians of the future.

https://www.quantamagazine.org/peter-scholze-and-the-future-...

↳ reply 1 — happy-go-lucky:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Scholze

> Scholze was a student of Rapoport, who was a student of Deligne, who was a student of Grothendieck, who was a student of Schwartz; in this chain, Scholze, Deligne, Grothendieck, and Schwartz are all Fields medallists.

↳ reply 2 — FuriouslyAdrift:

Ramanujan is another one that did much in his head and lacked a lot of formality in his methods. Many intuitive mathematicians are this way (Shinichi Mochizuki is another although his work may just be so hard for others to undertsand that it appears to lack rigor).

Top #3 — wqtz:

Ahhh, epistemology... Does any academic researcher even care about these things anymore?

If you're in academia, you've probably noticed a major shift recently. Research production at an industrial scale through AI.

Grants have "always" been awarded to professors based on quantity multiplied by quality. Now, some professors are churning out 1–3 papers a month with the same group of co-authors. All the grant money goes to them. Grant givers are just only counting the numbers of papers being published.

The Industrial Revolution has hit academia, and some academics are busy arguing for the artisanal value of research while some are creating factories for research.

↳ reply 1 — jltsiren:

I've seen a modest increase in productivity in bioinformatics. While the field is computational, it's ultimately about analyzing physical processes. The biggest bottlenecks have always been figuring out what makes sense to do and getting the data you need.

You can of course try new ideas and make software tools much faster now, but software is much like meetings. They can be productive if properly motivated, but they can also be a way to pretend you are working without contributing anything of real value.

Theoretical computer science and mathematics have changed. I'm not sure if they will remain active fields of research in the future. If they will, I would guess that theorems and proofs will eventually become things you include as supplementary data rather than in the main paper. Outside some rare exceptions, people may not consider them publishable results anymore.

↳ reply 2 — Loquebantur:

Yes, true scientists do care about epistemology.

The problem is the systemic disincentivation of true science, the pursuit of truth and knowledge unencumbered by greed.

When you speak favorably of "factories for research", you adopt the position of a mindless consumer, relishing the prospect of "abundant" products of science.

You fail to notice, livestock lives in abundance as well.

item.title: Kitty 0.50
item.description: 342 points, 213 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (sw.kovidgoyal.net)

→ HN comments  ·  342 points  ·  213 comments

Top #1 — JonnieCache:

The shader support offers a hook to trigger on the bell character, so of course I had to hook this up to a screenshake shader. Get fish to emit a bell on a nonzero command exit, and I have screenshake on failed commands. I expected this to be really annoying but it's actually kindof great:

https://jcd.pub/2026/11/04/screenshake-shaders-for-kitty/

↳ reply 1 — dyingkneepad:

Completely off-topic, but here we go: look at how your site renders on a very-wide monitor. My browser (Firefox Desktop) is 2560 pixels wide, and 100% of your website content is on the right side of the screen. item.title: The lost malloc()
item.description: 144 points, 59 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (napcakes.nekoweb.org)

→ HN comments  ·  144 points  ·  59 comments

Top #1 — adrian_b:

The author did not really find from where SIMULA 67 had taken "new".

In November 1965, C.A.R. Hoare published an extremely influential paper: "Record Handling". This was a proposed extension for the successor of ALGOL 60.

Almost all of the features that were added in SIMULA 67 over its predecessor, the SIMULA language, come directly from the paper of Hoare, with two big exceptions: class inheritance and the "virtual" procedures, which were invented by the SIMULA 67 creators (Kristen Nygaard & Ole-Johan Dahl) and which are essential for object-oriented programming.

The SIMULA 67 keywords "class" and "new" were taken from Hoare's paper (Hoare actually had taken "class" from COBOL 60, which used a very different terminology in comparison with ALGOL 60, among the many differences being the use of "class" instead of the "type" used by ALGOL 60).

Hoare's paper discussed a lot of programming language features, most of which were new, including defining structured types with constructors and destructors, discriminated unions (taken from John McCarthy), enumerations, the NULL pointer and many others.

SIMULA 67 was one of the first languages which implemented many of the features proposed by Hoare. Other languages that implemented some of the proposed features were IBM PL/I, ALGOL 68, then a couple of years later, in 1970-11, Pascal.

The keyword "new" had already been used for the first time by Niklaus Wirth, but at Wirth it had a different meaning than at Hoare. It declared a variable that was local to a block, which would hide any old variable with the same name that had been declared outside that block. So "new" at Wirth was equivalent with "auto" and "register" of the language C.

Later, in the language Pascal, Wirth abandoned his original use of "new", replacing it with the "new" introduced by Hoare.

Top #2 — OskarS:

> Not only that, mfree() receives the size of the object it is deallocating, as it should.

I've always thought that one of the biggest tiny mistakes in the history of this industry. It means, more or less, that you're forcing the memory allocator to keep track of these sizes when it shouldn't have to. There's virtually no sensible case where the person calling free() doesn't know the size of the allocation, so now we're keeping that book-keeping twice, in "user-space" and inside the memory allocator. Like, think about the cases when you'd call malloc:

* For allocating a single object of type T, the size is just `sizeof(T)`, so you can just pass that to free()

* For allocating an array of objects, the size is `count * sizeof(T)`, and I can't think of a single time where you DON'T know what `count` is. It's either statically sized (in which case it's just a constant), or if you have a dynamically growing array, you need to keep track of the reserved space to know when you reallocate. If nothing else, you need it for bounds-checking.

* For chunks of raw memory, you also presumably know when deallocating what the size of the raw memory you allocated is, for the same reasons as the previous point. Like, just having a raw char* pointer lying around with no size information is just terrible C practice.

If you truly don't know the size of your allocation (very hard to imagine when this would ever happen), you should be forced on the user-side to keep track of it somehow, not delegate that to the allocator.

It's a tiny amount of overhead, but it's for EVERY SINGLE MEMORY ALLOCATION since like 1975. Imagine how many times malloc() and free() has called since then! How much electricity, CPU usage, and memory has been wasted! It boggles the mind!

↳ reply 1 — wahern:

C2y has already added free_sized, FWIW, which is symmetrical with malloc. See 7.25.4.7 in the latest draft at https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n3998.pdf

It also adds free_aligned_sized as the counterpart to C11's aligned_alloc. Though while you can pass memory from aligned_alloc to free, you can't use free_sized or free_aligned_sized with aligned_alloc'd or malloc'd memory respectively, a potential (and unavoidable?) foot gun.

↳↳ reply — dooglius:

But if you still have to support the plain free functions it doesn't help because you'd still have to track the information anyway.

↳↳↳ reply — wahern:

The degree to which it helps or not depends on the implementation. For example, free could be a slow path that does extra bookkeeping lookups the sized variants wouldn't need to. Large allocations and non-default aligned allocations often use different bookkeeping data structures from how most allocations are handled internally anyhow. In such cases that check needs to be done up front, and at least on virtual memory systems (where it's relatively easy to segregate allocations types by VM range) it doesn't much matter whether you're indexing that first level directory based on pointer or size.

But, yeah, it's not an ideal situation from the perspective of free_aligned advocates.

↳ reply 2 — adrian_b:

Many allocators must keep 2 sizes for every allocated object: the size of the allocated memory and the size actually occupied by the requested object.

Some allocators keep other extra information for each object. Thus they need all that information and if the "memory free" function gives them only the size of the object, that is not enough.

Since the size is not enough, it is superfluous for the user program to provide it. When given a pointer to an object, the memory allocator will know where to find all the associated data. It might be in the cache line that is immediately before the pointed memory, or it might be in an array, at an index that can be deduced somehow from the value of the pointer, or all the information might be implicit, e.g. when objects are allocated from stacks of objects of the same size, when the size can be deduced from the pointer value, so it is not stored anywhere.

Therefore the correct definition for a memory free function is to have only a pointer as parameter, to give freedom to the allocator to use whichever strategy is deemed better.

Top #3 — tptacek:

Malloc implementations are anything but boring!

https://csapp.cs.cmu.edu/3e/docs/dsa.pdf

item.title: C++26 Disapproved
item.description: 361 points, 257 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (andreasfertig.com)

→ HN comments  ·  361 points  ·  257 comments

Top #1 — jandrewrogers:

As someone who writes high-reliability C++ but is completely outside the standards process, I see the issues with C++ Contracts. It isn’t clear that it solves a problem that anyone has in real codebases, especially after C++20 concepts.

If you were already writing high-reliability C++ then the benefits are difficult to quantify. If you weren’t writing high-reliability C++ then it saves you almost nothing over doing the standard idioms of high-reliability C++ that were already available to you at very marginally more cost. It does standardize expression of it in narrow cases but the payoff seems minimal.

Most of what C++ Contracts delivers is a mashup of what you can already do with constexpr and C++20 Concepts. I like reliability features but this feature, as delivered, looks fairly useless if you already use reliability features. A compelling standard would need to make much deeper guarantees out of the box. And the compiler can already see through most compositions of constexpr and C++20 concepts, which is already very expressive.

C++ Contracts looks a bit like a feature that was designed long before current standard features existed.

↳ reply 1 — throwaway2037:

    > high-reliability
I never heard this term used with C++ before. Can you explain more? Ideally: Can you give an example snip of code that demonstrates it clearly?

↳↳ reply — zaphirplane:

↳↳↳ reply — Rexxar:

↳ reply 2 — drivebyhooting:

Your comment just made me realize contracts is different from concepts (which are basically bounded genetics, right…?)

↳ reply 3 — pjmlp:

The problem is that the current design doesn't take into account binary libraries, or what happens when conflicting contract modes are linked together, as contracts aren't reflected on ABI.

Additionally they offer very little mechanisms versus Eiffel's original design, Ada/SPARK or Frama-C.

A basic MVP, expected to improve on subsequent C++ version, assuming that the proposal authors stick around for those evolution proposals.

Top #2 — nanolith:

While I can understand that C++ contracts were met with controversy, contract annotations scoped at analysis time that can be verified by external tools, such as static analyzers, model checkers, or automatic theorem provers, are incredibly useful.

I put together an alternative function contract and invariant mechanism in C using CBMC and custom macros that effectively allows me to perform formal methods in C using compositional verification. The reason why I chose C is because of its relative simplicity and relative ease of building tooling around it. C++ contracts provide some feature parity, and would let me take advantage of some of the features in C++ relative to C.

I hope that the contract proposal is workshopped and simplified so it can be proposed again for a future version. Its current form is unsuitable, but it deserves a second chance with a simpler implementation. Contracts would narrow the safety gap between C++ and languages such as Ada / SPARK.

↳ reply 1 — uecker:

C and formal verification is an awesome combination. I tried cmbc on some toy programs, it it fully automatically proved memory safety and all assertions. But for larger programs one has to split up with a contract-like facility.

Can you tell us more how you use cbmc with macros? I am also exploring this.

I also wonder what feature from C++ you miss in C?

↳ reply 2 — twhitmore:

Contracts are useful, but don't guaranteed anything if type safety & memory safety can be bypassed.

I think the ISO panel made the right call. The real world consider memory safety & execution integrity to already be critical issues (and C++ no longer to be viable), and they are correct. The WG has its priorities wrong.

Top #3 — LugosFergus:

I get why some folks would like to see contracts in the language, but C++ is also buckling due to the shear complexity that's getting tacked on to it. I'd rather see more proposals such as C++26's "erroneous behavior" that attempts to reign in the language's shortcomings.

Not that just learning basic neural networks but the two book don't appear to cover the same ground.

item.title: Safari introduces Adaptive Dark Mode in 27.3
item.description: 370 points, 206 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (webkit.org)

→ HN comments  ·  370 points  ·  206 comments

Top #1 — kickingvegas:

FYI, light-dark() in CSS is a thing now.

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/V...

↳ reply 1 — kps:

And `:prefers-color-scheme` has been supported by all major browsers for seven years.

↳↳ reply — cosmotic:

Windows 3 through windows 7 had pervasive support for dark mode as long as application developers didn't custom paint their user interfaces. Application developers started out almost all supporting system colors and gradually over the next 25 years or so started implementing their own custom-drawn interfaces, accelerated by embedded IE/mshtml views and then later even more by Electron. This concluded with practically zero interfaces supporting the system color scheme.

↳↳↳ reply — Melatonic:

Maybe the apps with the windows classic interface. I remember it starting mainly around the XP days when alls started designing these super ugly (but trendy at the time) rounded corner and bubbly interfaces that were static in resolution and colour scheme.

↳ reply 2 — akersten:

It makes me so angry that they named the CSS function `light-dark` instead of leaving the door open to allowing generic user- or site-specified color schemes. I mean it was right there in all the other mechanisms around this feature, they just had to read and think about why these are structured the way they are, and why "light" and "dark" were always values and not keywords in all of these..:

    - <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">
    
    - :root { color-scheme: light dark }

    - @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { }

    - <picture><source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)">
.... and then we've got `light-dark()`, the goofy looking dragon hanging out to the side of these majestic, forward-thinking parts of the specification.

Did they not look at the prior art and notice that "one of these things is not like the other?" All the other pieces of this puzzle, conceivably, could have one day had something like `:root { color-scheme: halloween }` or `@media (prefers-color-scheme: supercontrast)` but no, we're just going to cement `light-dark()` as the only two possible color schemes we'd ever want to switch between forever.

Top #2 — greazy:

Everyone should checkout Dark Reader extension, it's been doing adaptive dark mode for many years, and it's customisable. It even does light mode too. Using it in Firefox on HN right now!

↳ reply 1 — ckdot:

Slows down loading of websites a lot though.

↳ reply 2 — chrisra:

I'm concerned that these extensions can "read and modify" everything. I can't use that for work.

Top #3 — JulianPaul:

Am I still the only one who doesn't use dark mode? My astigmatism can't take it

↳ reply 1 — MBCook:

No. It’s stupid. There’s a reason we don’t write white text on black paper. There’s a reason the first Mac showing black text on a white background was such an improvement.

I don’t get the point at all (and don’t want to hear it, I’ve seen the arguments before).

It’s nice it’s there for people who want it but it baffles me it’s constantly treated like the greatest thing ever.

↳↳ reply — echoangle:

> There’s a reason we don’t write white text on black paper.

Because wood is bright and you can’t really print white ink on a black paper?

There might be a usability advantage but using black ink on white paper doesn’t really prove that, that’s just the easier option of the two possible choices.

↳↳↳ reply — MBCook:

It’s easier, sure. Especially at first. But we’ve had paper for a while now. Different colors of ink too. If light text on dark background was superior, we would be using it. And could have for hundreds of years for anything considered important.

↳ reply 2 — steve1977:

Yeah same here, the only time I use dark mode is usually when I feel a migraine attack might be coming up (and I get very sensitive to light)

item.title: US tech giants' hidden AI debt swells 90% to $3.2T in 6 months
item.description: 319 points, 139 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (asia.nikkei.com)

→ HN comments  ·  319 points  ·  139 comments

Top #1 — ggm:

I very much hope this, and other threads on the financially insane behaviour of the tech sector get more surface. I don't think having this die in "new" is helpful because this stuff, the norms of how business looks at the balance sheet and decides what is, and is not rational business investment, this stuff is -> important <-

This is a significant proportion of the market. Having this amount of money not understood is harmful.

↳ reply 1 — zenincognito:

Althlough one might argue they are sitting on a lot of cash.

↳↳ reply — repeekad:

They're sitting on non-cancellable commitments from Anthropic and OpenAI, which once public will become the markets problem while employees and private equity walk home paid.

↳ reply 2 — chermi:

What do you want? Some oversight board voting on what companies are allowed to do with their own money?

Wtf are the downvotes. It's a question.

Top #2 — whatever1:

The company budgets cannot sustain this. Behemoths like Google and Amazon with insane balance sheets are now on their knees begging for loans.

We (as a country) should contain our exposure to this insanity. If companies want to go bankrupt let them go, but we cannot strangle the liquidity of the entire market to feed the ambitions of these handful of companies.

↳ reply — forgetfreeman:

Apparently we can? Anyway, y'all think it's too soon to pivot into precious metals?

Top #3 — treis:

This is quite misleading. It includes numbers for commitments for leases of data centers and payments for power that are decades into the future.

Even if AI completely busts and all of these servers are worthless that doesn't mean the data centers are. There's still a need for data centers to host non-AI servers. The hyperscalers will close/sell other data centers and serve from places where they have long term commitments at.

3.2 trillion sounds like a lot until you spread it over 20 years and half a dozen trillion+ dollar companies. It's hard to tell how much a bag they're holding but it's almost certainly negligible compared to revenue and market cap. The only real systemic risk is the risk of for some reason not needing any data centers.

↳ reply 1 — vessenes:

As I've been pointing out a little bit recently -- the 'downside' scenario -- somehow we conclude we have enough inference at our world's desired quality and therefore demand stabilizes below that of these datacenters -- would be GREAT for the world. Super cheap intelligence for all.

If some lenders go bankrupt on a datacenter note post-buildout and the capital structure is reworked, lowering the costs by removing capitalization costs from the cashflow of the inference provider, that is all to the good of people who did not do the initial lending.

I think that is extremely unlikely, but it's good for datacenter doomers to think through these scenarios IMO.

↳↳ reply — nickff:

Your take seems a bit optimistic if we use the dot-com boom as an analogy. The dot-com boom sped up a massive infrastructure build-out, but also left damage that lasted for a very long time, with many organizations collapsing, and others taking a very long time to recover (e.g. cisco networks). It also seems that these 'data-centers' have a higher depreciation rate than 'dark-fiber' did post-dot-com, which means that there is likely to be greater capital waste.

I am not sure whether the dot-com boom was a net-positive, and the AI boom may be less productive.

↳↳↳ reply — vessenes:

It absolutely was a net positive. On the infrastructure side we got datacenters built and tons of dark fiber put down. At the start of the boom we had only 2G cellular for goodness sake. I think you could argue we wouldn't have necessarily had the rise in cloud compute without some of the 'overbuilding' of datacenters in web 1.

For reference this 'massive build-out' resulted in, according to a Berkeley study I found, 500MW of total datacenter power in the US across 320 locations at end of 2020. This wasn't too much for very long: as of 2005, according to Tier1 there were 511 datacenters. And it was likely only really a year or two: Dupont's VA3 utilization numbers published it at 50% utilization in 2003, 89.4% in 2004, then full thereafter.

Meanwhile, these infrastructure improvements allowed, for example, things like the iPhone to be built and deployable -- there was 3g, there were a LOT more web devs that could create the early (web only) apps the iPhone needed to compete. This in turn allowed another round of investment to be built on top of all of that.

On the capital side, investors were also able to buy Amazon at around $1 / share. AAPL at iPhone launch was $7/share. I haven't split adjusted either of these, this is just from memory.

I don't think a bust was necessarily good but the boom undeniably built out infrastructure, a small fraction of what the world is currently using, and did it pretty quickly, and then post bust that infra got bought out in a capital efficient manner. I think that's the bear case here.

Put another way, the Dotcom one boom was wrong about two things: timing was too fast, and the predicted scale of change was way, way, way too small. They undersold the future.

↳ reply 2 — Grimblewald:

what do you think debt is? what you've described as misleading, is debt by definition.

“Multi-WAN network toolkit — connect up to 5 uplinks. Configure dynamic routing, failover, load balancing, and firewall rules. Use it simultaneously as a Wi‑Fi hotspot and client. Tunnel traffic through a VPN and multiple gateways. ”

wouldn't a VPN (on your phone or laptop) solve this?

Top #2 — vr46:

I already nabbed my coupon for the pre-order last week - looks super cool!

My F0 is always close at hand, doing everything from being my go-to trigger for whatever random thing I'm playing with, to being an instant output for any signal I'm trying to read. Plus it's a really fun educational tool for myself and various kids around - I keep a load of little NFC 216 tags around, in my bag, in a pouch attached to my Mac, and showing both young and old how to use them, and read them with the phone, leads to conversations about treasure hunts, hiding them in the pub, showing counters with amusing messages...

We used it as a metronome the other day with its blue light, and on the flip side I've been looking at ways to integrate it into my EDC as a modern key, or a programmable keyring. It isn't super-secure, but that does make it easier to work with.

I'm excited about the F1, mainly curious about its logic analyzer capabilities, since I'm actually designing and building one - even it is fifty times worse than a commercial one, I just want to know how they work. And these little devices help find out how other things work.

Top #3 — mncharity:

Even when working from a fixed desk, I appreciate alternating desk work with strolling-thinking, when the environment permits it. Now, with incoming HMDs capable of laptop-like angular resolution, I've been exploring what an all-day NYC wander-and-pause setup/build might look like. Mobile local computes are easier now than they've ever been. Perhaps a SFF PC with multiple snap on MCIO/quick-disconnect-water GPUs+radiators? But agentic power demands... strolling with rolling battery luggage? Eep.

So perhaps ultra-light instead, a cloud PC, and always-on mobile networking to it? Multiplexing multiple cellular providers, and wifi? Perhaps with panel and cantennas. And... clueful juggling of the local wireless environment?

To get "for a better signal, I should walk along here rather than there"? Accumulating a personal neighborhood heat map? Or maybe "neat, in this weather, a cantenna gets library community wifi from across the river"? Or ...?

Wireless environment awareness has long seemed to me a fun concept, but with unclear use cases. It just now occurred to me this might be one? If not the Flipper One necessarily, something...

↳↳ reply — AceJohnny2:

item.title: How I use AI (Oct 2026)
item.description: 212 points, 247 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (ben.stolovitz.com)

→ HN comments  ·  212 points  ·  247 comments

Top #1 — mef51:

I always find so much cognitive dissonance in these kinds of posts.

> My most successful work this year was hand-writing a tool, replacing ~4,000 lines of vibe-code with a few hundred. My system has proven more flexible, easier to test, and more generalizable than what it replaced.

> agents still need human taste and experience to produce good work.

Where do you think human taste and experience in software comes from?

> overstimulating & exhausting in a way that coding never was.

> for many of us, honing the code, finding the right design, seeing the parts mesh together — that was the meditative purpose we found in our jobs.

> That’s not the only time AI waylaid me. LLMs could not figure out how to annotate that model’s training data correctly. I spent days going back and forth with them

> LLMs are not yet good companions when brainstorming complicated things.

Why do we expect this to get better? The training data will degrade in quality if more people rely on LLMs so I'd expect models to eventually start getting worse even if they currently enjoy apparent improvements in output.

> Writing code is solved.

What a strange thing to say given all the above experiences, which I think we all share.

Why are we willing to give up so much in terms of purpose and understanding for perceived productivity gains?

↳ reply 1 — bodge5000:

> The training data will degrade in quality if more people rely on LLMs so I'd expect models to eventually start getting worse even if they currently enjoy apparent improvements in output.

Its not a direct analogy, but this seems to me as like saying "I already know maths and english, why do we still hire and pay teachers". Its a massive issue that just seems to be hand-waved away as "we'll figure it out later".

To compound on the problem as well, even those of us who do still write code by hand are actively discouraged from sharing it, knowing no human will ever read it and we'll never be credited for our work, it'll just go in the pockets of a few big AI companies. I suppose there will be some that take some pride in knowing their code is helping AI models advance, but thats a small pool of an already small pool, assuming most people decide to just use the AI to write the code for them. A minority of a minority.

I guess this is the chickens coming home to roost of this whole attitude towards growth now, fallout later

↳ reply 2 — ramigb:

I am not OP, obviously, but I am writing to address the "Where do you think human taste and experience in software comes from?" point, hoping that I provide an alternative perspective.

As someone who wrote code for 27 years in all sorts of languages, not necessarily impressive code, but got paid for it, made a career, and changed life for the better multiple times, I don't think coding was ever an important part of the journey! Maybe it's cognitive dissonance, as you wrote above, but I believe taste comes from exploration, from trial and error, from being willing to be open and change old ways if new ways can improve how things are done!

Similar to taste in food or even music! You might think certain foods taste bad, but until you taste them, you won't be certain! Sometimes your senses will be right and the food will taste horrible; other times, you'll be fairly surprised. Similar to music—it's my life hobby—you might think certain genres or artists are bad, but until you sit down, give them a shot, and hear what they have to say, you won't know for certain if your judgment is correct.

If you meant by your comment that you need to code a lot to acquire taste and experience in software, I respectfully disagree. You are not completely wrong, though, but putting emphasis on code, if that's what you were going for, is an overstatement of code's importance. For that particular case, similar to the analogies mentioned above, it's about exploration and trying different languages, paradigms, solutions, and stacks, and unfortunately, we as humans have finite time, so we can't be trying and exploring fast enough to form judgments!

What I genuinely love about LLMs is mostly their exploratory powers. I try new stuff that I always wanted to try with actual products and form opinions about the whole experience.

Anyways, as I finished writing this, I realized, as always, I might be wrong! You might be right, taste is highly subjective! And acquiring it is a very personal thing! So I don't think right or wrong are important here!

↳ reply 3 — yewenjie:

> The training data will degrade in quality if more people rely on LLMs so I'd expect models to eventually start getting worse even if they currently enjoy apparent improvements in output.

RL is not dependent on training data. The mathocalypse didn't happen because they found better training data somewhere.

Top #2 — Daunk:

I believe that anyone who says that writing code is no longer needed, was probably not a very good coder to begin with. I have seen what the best models can do, and I've seen what people call "good", and I am not impressed.

However, I'm still split. Because this could mean that we see a jump in code quality, due to bad coders getting someone better to code for them. But we could see a decrease in code quality, due to less people "caring".

↳ reply 1 — LeafItAlone:

> I believe that anyone who says that writing code is no longer needed, was probably not a very good coder to begin with. I have seen what the best models can do, and I've seen what people call "good", and I am not impressed.

I envy you.

I believe that anyone who holds this position has been extremely lucky/fortunate to work with only top-tier developers. And does not read or work with open source projects.

Last year’s models are producing code better than _at least_ 50% of the developers I’ve worked with. Today’s frontier models are better than probably 75%. If the code that humans have been generating has been “good” (on average) or at least good enough, then the models that exist today are producing “good” code.

↳ reply 2 — Seattle3503:

Most people I've seen saying coding is solved are ML engineers who write throw away code for running one-off experiments. If you can effectively "archive" code after getting the results you need, I can see why you would say coding is solved. Sustainment is a non issue.

Top #3 — Dzugaru:

There is no substitute for reading the code in many many cases. I spend more than 3k/mo on tokens. I find incorrect assumptions baked into the code (the ultimate spec) and missed by the agents and tests daily. This is more pronounced in data analysis and complex systems.

As a side effect having to read the code at least once inevitably makes it way shorter and usually much better.

↳ reply 1 — prmph:

Exactly, I see insidious errors made by Claude Opus daily, all the time. Errors that would be very hard to catch with tests, because usually they are architectural level issues.

↳ reply 2 — geocar:

> I spend more than 3k/mo on tokens.

Dude you should buy tin. I can get you a banger box for $30k.

GLENDOWE: I can call spirits from the vasty deep.

> I can interpret weights too, but will that interpretation be correct?

Chances are much higher than a model can figure out what the patterns are, decipher them, and retain that knowledge in a meaningful way it can reason about. Me and you might take years or months to do all of that on our own, with a "map" of the weight we might be able to discuss it, but not as effortlessly as an LLM.

Thinking about it, it makes a lot of sense that LLMs could easily be trained to interpret weights. The attention mechanism of an LLM is very well suited to analyze a set of weights (in text form), since the attention to each weight in the text via key/query can sort of emulate the connection structure of the network that the weights represent.

This thing can accomplish the same results as the frontier models do, if you are willing to play a role of an higher level architect or decision maker. Guide it a bit here and there like a tech lead and you get everything done.

item.title: Postman silently auto-installs AI plugins and attempts to share all API data
item.description: 1146 points, 376 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  1146 points  ·  376 comments

Top #1 — primitivesuave:

Postman logs detailed information on every single API request you make through its tool, including query parameters. If you use the templating syntax `{{some_secret}}` to fill in a query parameter, it sends the actual secret content of `some_secret` to Postman's servers. If you disable outgoing network traffic to this logging endpoint, the entire app will stop working properly.

I discovered this when investigating whether Postman is HIPAA-compliant (it is not).

↳ reply 1 — wackget:

That sounds all sorts of illegal, and all sorts of immoral.

Did you flag it / create an issue?

↳↳ reply — primitivesuave:

Yes - I wrote some public posts, and a Medium article which I forgot about until just now: https://anonymousdata.medium.com/postman-is-logging-all-your...

My main point was that I wouldn't want my secrets to ever be sent to Postman under any circumstance (or alternately, stop calling them "secret"). A lot of the online responses were some variation of "why are you sending secrets in query parameters in the first place?" (I'm not). When I posted on Reddit, it escalated to targeted harassment by people who were obviously current/former employees at Postman.

I did send out an email blast to a bunch of CIOs/CSOs in my network which went a bit "email viral" through forwarding, and this ended up triggering a substantial amount of enterprise cancellations.

↳↳↳ reply — lelandfe:

> some variation of "why are you sending secrets in query parameters in the first place?" (I'm not)
