item.title: Study estimates 75% of NFL players who died over 15-year span had CTE
item.description: 258 points, 227 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (nbcnews.com)

→ HN comments  ·  258 points  ·  227 comments

Top #1 — cmiles8:

I would never let my child play contact football. The data is beyond clear that this sport causes irreparable life altering damage to the brain.

A lot of football players also suffer from mental health issues which, not to state the obvious, is likely not helped by banging your head all the time.

↳ reply 1 — chrisBob:

I am surprised by the otherwise intelligent and caring parents I have met who had their elementary schoolers playing tackle football. I don't understand that decision at all.

↳↳ reply — scoofy:

I grew up in Texas when football was basically religion. My parents flatly forbid me from playing. Any other sport was fine, no football. Every single person I knew on the team ended up with at least some kind of minimal, permanent injury. This was a decade before there were publications about CTE.

I'm quite thankful that I never ended up on the team, and think the entire concept of high school football is incredibly stupid given what we know about CTE.

↳ reply 2 — pton_xd:

I tried contact football in 7th grade and only lasted a few practice sessions. I was shocked by what I saw; other kids throwing their bodies into each other as if they were just bags of meat, sometimes colliding head-on. The ferocity with which they did it seemed like a source of pride for them and there was this sense of one-upmanship on who could tackle the best. The whole thing felt insane to me and I backed out immediately. I was involved in other sports like baseball and basketball so I was used to competitiveness, but nothing on that level of disregard for safety.

↳ reply 3 — pwthornton:

Play flag football. It's a great sport without the terrible risks. It's also being played by girls too.

I coach middle school girls. It's a blast. It has by far the most strategy of any youth sport.

If I had sons, I wouldn't let them play tackle football before high school, and I would have to think long and hard about that even.

I enjoyed flag football as a coach so much that I built my own play creation and team management software (https://getplaylook.com). One of the things that you get with flag at an early age because you aren't so focused on the physical side of the game is a higher emphasis on technique, particularly route running, and play design. Good play design can scheme people open, even if your team isn't very fast.

Top #2 — ggreer:

Here's a link to the study.[1] Since CTE can only be diagnosed by slicing up the brain, and former NFL players only tend to donate their brains to study if they're experiencing cognitive issues, there's obviously a bias in the sample. They tried to adjust for this by looking at rates of cognitive impairment in NFL players who donated their brains versus those who didn't. The ratio varied from 1.8x to 4x depending on age at death.

Unfortunately the number of brains studied isn't large enough to determine whether different positions have different levels of CTE. I'd guess that kickers would have very low risk compared to other positions, as they are rarely involved in collisions. Their stats hint that is the case, but the p-values are ridiculously high due to the small sample size.

1. https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle...

↳ reply — SkyPuncher:

This is good analysis. My only contribution is kickers CTE rates are likely correlated to CTE rates for soccer players. A lot of youth kickers are soccer players that decide to kick.

While soccer doesn’t tend to have as many concussion level impacts, there’s a lot of evidence that repeated sub-concussive impacts are just as bad.

↳↳ reply — ggreer:

I'd guess that CTE rates for football kickers are lower than for professional soccer players, as the rules forbid tackling or even running into them. A soccer player who becomes a football kicker will probably transition in high school at the latest. The total number of times they hit the ball with their head will be much lower than a career soccer player, and they'll stop doing it before players get stronger and kick the ball harder.

Kickers do kickoffs, extra points, and field goals. Besides that they're not on the field. The only time hitting a kicker is allowed is if it's some sort of fake play where the kicker ends up running with the ball. Even then, there tends to be a gentleman's agreement where teams won't rough up the opposing kicker, as doing so means their own kicker is fair game.

I knew one guy who was a kicker for a PAC-12 team (back when it was the PAC-10). He said he was hit only once in 4 years. Earlier in the game he'd insulted someone on the other team, and the next time they were both on the field, the guy hit him from behind long after the whistle blew. That's not really a football injury as much as it's a violent crime.

As far as I'm aware, no kicker has ever been found to have CTE (though the sample size for them is very small), and their concussion rates are much lower than average. I think the studies on kicker concussion rates overestimate how often they sustain head injuries, as they likely incorporate data from less competitive colleges and high schools where kickers also play other positions.

Top #3 — retrac:

Don't forget the hearing loss and tinnitus, too. Boxers and footballers tend to go deaf.

https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2014/07/140707134223.h...

> Leonetti recently spoke to retired players alongside EarQ at a meeting of the Chicago chapter of the NFL Players Association. When Leonetti asked how many players had experienced concussions during their career, they all raised their hands. When Leonetti asked how many have experienced hearing loss approximately 25 percent raised their hands. When he asked how many have tinnitus approximately 50 percent raised their hands.

item.title: AI is destroying my CS degree
item.description: 125 points, 117 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (lordtoots.bearblog.dev)

→ HN comments  ·  125 points  ·  117 comments

Top #1 — tcdent:

> It's been a huge learning curve.

I have been doing this professionally for over twenty years, and I still learn something every day. Over the past couple years, with AI augmentation, I learn even more, move faster and go deeper into the systems that I work on.

A CS degree was never going to provide you with all of the tools that you need for a successful career. It provided you with the basics to get your foot in the door.

AI is not replacing you or an education. AI is raising the bar of what you can comprehend and retain. From someone who is technically minded (and self-taught), all I have ever wanted is to keep learning.

↳ reply 1 — pantsforbirds:

> AI is not replacing you or an education. AI is raising the bar of what you can comprehend and retain. From someone who is technically minded (and self-taught), all I have ever wanted is to keep learning.

AI is, in my opinion, absolutely murdering the junior dev market. It's now much more efficient to pay for a senior or staff engineer and set them up with a subscription to claude or codex. I think things are going to remain fine for senior+ engineers, but I genuinely don't know what advice I'd give to graduating devs at this time.

↳↳ reply — reasonableklout:

Yep, and we have hard data on this: https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/08/ai-is-hitting-entry-level...

> Stanford researchers find the employment trends they identified for entry-level workers last year are persisting and expanding. Specifically, employment levels for workers ages 22 to 25 in the most “AI-exposed” occupations are now 19 percent below those of their peers in fields less exposed to AI disruption.

↳ reply 2 — wilkommen:

Many people in the tech world seem to espouse a great love for "always learning", but the way in which it is said always feels funny to me. Learn about what? When people say this, do they mean that they want to always be learning the next programming language, the next web framework, the next thick-client frontend web framework, the next python packaging CLI tool (pypi, virtualenv, uv ...), the next Linux distro? I'm tired of the churn. Most of these tools are not different enough from each other and don't have different enough use cases to be worth learning, but that's what a job in tech often seems to boil down to. You learn to do a basic set of tasks with one toolset, then once you get proficient, you swap all those tools out for another set of different tools that work completely differently but accomplish the same goal in a way that is not appreciably better or worse than the last set of tools. With AI, this will only get worse, as the cost for making new tools goes down. There seems to be a lot of churn just for the sake of churn.

↳ reply 3 — JaumeGreen:

> A CS degree was never going to provide you with all of the tools that you need for a successful career. It provided you with the basics to get your foot in the door.

Yes and no.

I concur that it was never about the tools, although I've seen plenty of people advocating it had a more "practical" approach, using the same tools as companies use, and in the same way.

On the other hand it's not only about the basics.

In there you can go at depth in aspects that you will have to fight to use, like proper engineering practices, and might only be vital on the later stages of your career. And I feel that those learnings, plus the possibility of acquiring a breadth of knowledge that is hardly possible otherwise, is what gives CS graduates a leg up to other practitioners of the art of software development.

YMMV and a leg up can be easily overtaken, yes.

Top #2 — dahart:

I’m hearing this more and more from both students and teachers. It seems like everyone in education is frustrated and can’t figure out how to use AI for education productively yet.

TBH I’m also thinking about how to use AI at work for learning. (My work environment is 100% all-in on AI.) Everyone can see and admit that AI coding is making us lazier and that it produces too much code to do old-style line by line reviews. Some people are using agent teams to churn out millions of lines of code where there’s zero hope of reviewing it. We don’t yet know how to keep quality high and complexity low while doing agent coding, we’re just having them write lots of tests and hoping that when things break they’re easy to fix. Agents should get better at broad architecture in the future, but they’re definitely not there yet.

> The amount of work involved has also tripled

This has to be one of the big ironies of using AI. I’ve heard this from other students too. The problem is that old-style assignments where the level of difficulty was hand-crafted is way way too easy for an LLM, therefore teachers need to crank the level of difficulty so the student has to actually spend some time on the assignment. But LLMs are getting better every month and the difficulty is so high that no students can possibly do the assignment by hand and now small errors in assignment design can lead to large errors in effort and time required.

↳ reply 1 — beej71:

> It seems like everyone in education is frustrated and can’t figure out how to use AI for education productively yet.

Oh, it's terrible. I'm a computer science instructor at a university (I have 20 years of industry experience prior) and it was already bad enough before trying to predict where the market was going to be 4 years in the future. But a year ago, it was tough to predict where the market was going to be in one month.

So yeah, we can teach all kinds of stuff. But is it the right stuff? With one month of visibility, who can tell?

But now I feel like it's settled down a little bit. And now I feel like I have more like 7 to 8 months of visibility. One thing that's helped is that we see the hiring differential between seniors and juniors. So now we can answer the question, what does the market want? It wants the expertise between junior and senior. And I'm confident it'll want that for at least the next 7-8 months.

Good luck cramming that into 4 years, though! I figure we have to try to bridge the gap as best we can. Eventually, seniors will become rare enough that the expense isn't worth it. It'll become better to hire cheaper most-qualified juniors.

There's still some seriously open-ended questions though. How much does coding matter, for example? If you ask senior devs who don't do any coding how much they rely on their coding expertise to make decisions, you'll get a zillion answers across the spectrum. This becomes even more true for senior devs who use AI for coding. Heck, ask 100 devs if it's important that you can even read code or not and see what comes out!

And then there's the question of how do you teach those systems level thinking skills? Historically, universities haven't taught those skills. You came out of the University with general problem solving skills in technology, and then at your job you were exposed to a small corner of the codebase to fix some bug. Gradually, over the years, you learn more and more of the codebase and become more and more senior. We have to get that into our curriculum. I'm working on that as we speak and will be working on that for the next several years, it looks like; even if my position vanishes, I'll keep attacking it—this is a tough problem that's fun to try to crack.

Anyway, I hope someday my forward visibility gets back up to 18 months. Won't that be amazing. I'd also like to buy some RAM. ;)

↳ reply 2 — visarga:

> We don’t yet know how to keep quality high and complexity low while doing agent coding, we’re just having them write lots of tests and hoping that when things break they’re easy to fix

Implement more versions with different languages, frameworks, libraries and AI agents. Then you can do differential execution for testing, which is easier than imagining testing scenarios from pure code. You can fuzz or use production data (shadow mode execution) to get notified early of divergences.

Keeping a population of diverse replicas might be the simplest way to derisk AI code. When 2 replicas diverge an agent can decide - was it a bug in one of them, or was the spec unclear? Either way, if you fix a bug or clarify the spec you come ahead.

A separate class of problems is related to intent divergence. For that my solution is to keep a full log of all user messages during the lifetime of the project. Even 10,000 messages collected over weeks and months can be read and summarized in a few minutes. That means you can check for intent divergence with agents, but you always start from the raw source (your human messages) not from intermediate summaries and diverged code.

Combining the 2 ideas would make each replica agent derive the user intent separately from the same log.

Top #3 — moomin:

Answers so far are assuming that this is complaining that their traditional CS course is not that useful for getting a job anymore.

That’s not what it’s about. It’s actually from someone who genuinely wants to learn for the sake of learning who’s talking about how AI is creating havoc in her studies.

↳ reply 1 — Aurornis:

This is a blog post where it’s easy to see which commenters did not read the blog before commenting.

The real villain in this story is the teaching staff. They need to get their act together and stop using generative AI for courseloads.

In other words, they need to do their job. The parts about AI mandates changing every 3 months reeks of an overly bureaucratic, admin-heavy structure where the students’ learning is a lower priority being performative about AI for your boss.

↳↳ reply — dieortin:

You don’t know what pressures the teaching staff is under.

↳↳↳ reply — Aurornis:

Neither do you, but either way that should not become their students' problem.

People have to do their jobs. Having AI generate slop and then sending it off to students or coworkers is not acceptable. It's not the students' problem to deal with things that may or may not be going on in the administration.

They're paying a lot of money to get an education and the university, as a whole, needs to do their job.

Saying that the teaching staff is under pressure excuses nothing. Students are paying for an education and it needs to be delivered at acceptable quality.

↳ reply 2 — hbn:

I would argue the job thing is more at risk and opportunity for learning is at an all time high. You've got 24/7 access to a very skilled personal tutor.

AI can teach you, you just have to put the effort in to tell it to teach you. In some contexts, I might want it to fire off a utility bash script and I have no interest in learning bash so I just run it and don't worry too much about the implementation. But if I'm getting it to help me write Java code for work, I review the output and ask it about parts that I don't understand. And it teaches me way better than the old way of reading dry/bad documentation.

It's what you make of it.

Somewhat related: did you know that you cannot disable GMail's GenAI features without disabling the traditional ML powered features, such as smart inbox, which predates LLMs? In this case, Google/Alphabet is conflating GenAI/LLMs with traditional machine learning, so you can't opt out of genai---which necessarily requires access to your data by the models---without deactivating the previous non-LLM powered features.

Which I get it, they indeed can use LLMs to improve the previous traditional ML pipeline. However I believe bundling these options together shouldn't be legal and I never expected Google to employ dark patterns like this. item.title: Charles Tandy, the mastermind behind Radio Shack
item.description: 125 points, 91 comments. See description for top comments.

Top #1 — geerlingguy:

Many fond memories of Radio Shack. I bought some electronics kits, a mini DJ setup, and many, many components there as a kid. At one time, they had quite a catalog of Radio Shack branded items that were "good but not great"... but more importantly available a few miles away within practically any city. Almost every mall in St. Louis had one (usually near a hobby train store or an arcade).

↳ reply 1 — EvanAnderson:

> ...but more importantly available a few miles away within practically any city.

We're around the same age and likely have similar memories. I poured over Radio Shack catalogs and weekly ads when I was a kid. When my family went to the local mall I'd make a beeline for the Radio Shack and play w/ the various computers there until my parents pried me away.

When I started doing PC tech work (in rural Western Ohio in the late 90s) it was always an option, no matter how far out in "the sticks" you were working, to drive to a Radio Shack for emergency parts. They might not have exactly what you needed, and you'd probably pay a hefty price, but you could get the job done.

That ubiquity definitely left an impression on IT technicians of my generation. I was recently doing some work w/ a legacy system that called for some serial gender-bender/null modem cables. Not having any handy I had to improvise with some DE-9 to RJ-45 hoods and creative crimping to get what I needed. A cow-orker commented "We used to be able to just go to Radio Shack when we needed stuff like that in a hurry."

item.title: The 'Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen' post is misleading
item.description: 855 points, 188 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (honnibal.dev)

→ HN comments  ·  855 points  ·  188 comments

Top #1 — bushido:

Speaking for myself. I’ve been aware of a lot of concepts around training, but stayed away from it until very recently.

A few weeks ago, I formed a hypothesis that I could get a smaller model good at the specific standards I have for my git commit messages, which are hard to get out of most LLMs today.

I spent the last four to five weeks on traditional training. It improved in a lot of areas, but not enough to be usable for me.

Yesterday, the article the author of this post is critical of gave me enough of an aha that maybe the problems I was seeing could be solved by having a larger LLM change the weights directly, without going through training.

In the last twelve-ish hours I’ve made more headway than I have in 2+ weeks. I’m using one of my last well performing checkpoints (full fine-tune + changes to the decision head/LoRA, etc.) and gave the model free rein to change any of the layers.

Its last two actions: (a) removed 16 participant-order directions from a head matrix, which improved one type of reasoning and degraded another, and (b) restored one of the 16, which reversed the degradation while keeping the core improvement.

All that to say, this might be known to people who’ve been around training for years, even decades, but it’s new to a lot of us. And we’re excited about it.

↳ reply 1 — rybosome:

> All that to say, this might be known to people who’ve been around training for years, even decades, but it’s new to a lot of us. And we’re excited about it.

I've done some training and fine-tuning for a few years, and the ideas here were new to me. I'm also having a breakthrough on a problem and am very excited about it.

There's a very narrow classification task which I've been building around Jev. The cost and latency of Jev are great, the accuracy is pretty good - definitely usable - but I disliked sending the data in this particular task off-box. Not a criticism of Typesafe, it's the nature of the task which is privacy oriented. I decided to see if a model whose weights were one-shotted by an LLM (the model architecture was designed thoughtfully ahead of time) could be competitive with a similarly architected but trained model, and both of those against Jev.

Results are early in my experiment, but it appears that a "vibe tuned" classifier consisting of weights small enough to run on a laptop GPU are competitive in accuracy and latency with Jev. The process hasn't even proceeded to the point of the trained models having meaningful results, and I already have something usable for an MVP.

Whatever may have been possible previously or was obvious to other people, the absurd efficacy of this process was not obvious to me. Emphasizing that this particular task was very narrowly defined, I still believe that this effortless model-building capability is a profound and exciting discovery.

↳ reply 2 — HappyDreamer:

> it’s new to a lot of us. And we’re excited about it.

Yes definitely.

Seems to me as if the weighs fit in the big model's context, it (the big model) reads all weights and doesn't need python.

But if the weights don't fit in context, then it uses python.

Isn't that pretty obvious in a way? That if too many weights, can't look at all. I don't think there's a need for OP to be dismissive when the AI uses python to look at a subset of the weights. It just has to?

To me, Astra understanding a 200k weights small model (the stuck car) is amazing enough already.

↳ reply 3 — O_H_E:

I'm even more clueless about the the field.

Those two types of reasoning, are those well definitely in the field generally, or are they mini-personal evals you run?

It has been frustrating trying to quantify why one pseudo-frontier model seems better at some non-coding tasks than another pseudo-frontier one.

Top #2 — neom:

I feel like a lot of this Astra editing Qwen stuff is regurgitation of existing relatively well known techniques, for example: https://arxiv.org/html/2406.11717v3 and conceptually similar to: https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.05648 (tho this is done in training iirc)

Top #3 — GavinAnderegg:

I'm still impressed by the "Weight-Space Programming" idea. Perhaps its because I didn't know that LLMs could understand or successfully modify weights at all previous to reading it. However, I think the examples provided in the original piece were eye-opening. Yes, humans can build tooling to modify weights, but the author here agrees that it's tough. The examples where Astra was interacting with weights are still novel, and Astra seemed to handle them with surprising ease.

↳ reply — syllogism:

Here's the work that shows how rule-based logic can be compiled into transformer weights:

* Thinking Like Transformers” by Weiss, Goldberg & Yahav (ICML 2021).: https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.06981

* Tracr: Compiled Transformers as a Laboratory for Interpretability https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.05062 (code at https://github.com/deepmind/tracr)

So it's not really an "LLMs can modify weights" thing. Rather it's "LLMs can write programs that can write or modify weights". Indeed LLMs can write many programs, it's impressive.

item.title: Revolut moves to self-hosted GLM
item.description: 182 points, 155 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (twitter.com)

→ HN comments  ·  182 points  ·  155 comments

Top #1 — littlecranky67:

"the gains showed up when tokens stopped being rationed" - I can totally see that. I am leading (as an external consultant) a larger dev team for a huge insurance company. The devs are quite junior or in general more the "I became a sw-eng here because that company is the only big employer in a 1h radius" type of people (meaning: No rockstar developers). Most of them do not play with AI in their spare time, and they have been told to spend claude tokens wisely. Everybody is too afraid now to play with it and explore during work hours for fear of being token shamed.

At the same time, most of their junior devwork can be replaced completely by AI - so they really should start to learn how to work with it. I recommended everybody to get a private 20€/month claude subscription and use it for toy projects. I have younger devs (early 20s) in the team that told me they won't spend private money, or simply have no usecase in their private life for AI. We talk about software engineers here, and IMHO most of them are in denial of the fact that their skills have mostly become worthless if they don't start to pivot to something valueable.

↳ reply 1 — grvdrm:

Would enjoy chatting offline if up for it. I am an external consultant acting as more of an operations/product lead to insurance, but come the insurance side.

Curious about consulting model? Are you external (full-time) lead or fractional? Embedded in their tech and security stack or just helping organize/lead through communication channels?

↳ reply 2 — mleroy:

Hey Opus 9, you are an insurance carrier offering web-based policies and servuces across the EU. Available tools: german_notary_api, bafin_compliance.

Here is €1B in initial capital. Go!

↳ reply 3 — Hamuko:

>I recommended everybody to get a private 20€/month claude subscription and use it for toy projects.

That's about 20€/month more than I care to give Anthropic. They already stole my data and now they want my money too? No thanks. I'll stick to running Gemma or Qwen on my Mac.

Top #2 — jacquesm:

We did the same thing, on much less powerful hardware but it has served us very well and we don't need to worry at all about the question whether or not the suppliers of inference services can be trusted long term with our data. The answer to that question in my opinion is 'absolutely not'.

↳ reply 1 — krona:

How do security conscious self-hosters sandbox their runtimes?

↳↳ reply — jacquesm:

By pulling the plug. This box simply has no pathway to the internet. I do pretend I have one and it's interesting to see what it tries to do. For instance, Qwen tends to try to hit ali related URLs for websearch and is very disappointed when the mothership is not responding. I've yet to catch a model on an exfiltration attempt, either they are so good at this that it escapes my scrutiny (possible but unlikely) or they are simply not doing it. I would bet on the last one. Just don't say you're working for the Tibet Liberation Frontier or the Keep Taiwan Independent movement.

↳ reply 2 — mkesper:

Can you share some details about your setup? Would probably be interesting for a lot of people.

Top #3 — redmalang:

For the past several months about 90% of the work we do goes to open source models. If you ignore the noise around 'cheap' etc, you might find that with a little extra effort to more precisely define what you need not only do these models generally work as well, and they will generally more closely follow instructions - on longer timeframes this is actually pretty helpful.

They are less good on ambiguous prompts like 'fix all the problems' (which to my chagrin is a very common prompt it turns out..)

↳ reply 1 — jacquesm:

Yes, that's a good point: you really need to work on the prompts, even if the harness is the same. Ambiguity is a real problem as is what we call 'the negative space', what isn't in the prompt but what is implied by the prompt to be undesirable. You need to spell that out in more detail it is not enough just to say 'do x' but you also need to make sure to say 'and not y or z', and knowing what y or z are requires a bit more insight into what hobby horses are encoded in a model.

To give one example: I'm doing a lot of stuff that involves hardware. When settings things up for fixing a bug I have to make sure to include that the hardware has been tested and works well. If I don't do that the model will almost certainly spend a ridiculous amount of time speculating about all the different ways in which the hardware could be broken (including theorizing about chip mask errors and all kinds of other obscure and rarely seen in practice defects). It's going to end up telling itself that for sure the 500 lines it just produced are absolutely perfect and the device that is on the i2c bus is broken in a way that it just really can't progress with solving the issue because there is nothing wrong with the code.

These kinds of blind-spots are funny when they happen once in a month but when they happen regularly it begins to be irritating. Adding a line or two to the prompt will take care of the issue. Frontier models tend to be better at this sort of thing.

↳↳ reply — redmalang:

Us too! Hardware is very interesting - I find in fact that 'smart' (aka expensive) models can overthink complex hardware state machines and end up doing atrocious code because it will try to handle every possible edge case (unbidden, mind you). What has worked very well is harvesting and aggregating lessons and feeding this automatically into our pi sessions, this allows the models which listen to instructions to avoid a lot of time burning tokens on internal dialogue to ascertain the nature of reality.. but the expensive ones: a) they dont listen b) they ironically know too much!

↳↳↳ reply — jacquesm:

Funny, I wonder how many people are retracing the same pathways. Another interesting one: asking for reboots or resets to start from a 'known state' even though this will not change a thing. But it's a quick path out of the trouble spot that might just work so why not try it. I've added the following line: "The hardware is on a spaceship and is impossible to access by an operator and for some reason they forgot to include reset logic, so we have to work with what we've got.". I've been gaslit by AI so often I figure I can return the favor without penalty.

↳ reply 2 — epolanski:

DS 4.1 flash 1017 is June's sota at such low pricing it doesn't matter how many tokens you're using.

item.title: Could a modern chess engine on a Pentium have defeated Kasparov in 1996?
item.description: 282 points, 135 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (nicholas.carlini.com)

→ HN comments  ·  282 points  ·  135 comments

Top #1 — tombert:

Very tangential, but I think a lot about how modern video compression has gotten so unbelievably good that if we went back in time with AV1 or HEVC or something, I'm wondering if we could have had passable video streaming at 240p with something like an ISDN connection.

It would be a tight fit, but I still think within feasibility. We've gotten so good at shrinking video that it kind of feels like wizardry to me. Granted, I'm not sure there existed a computer in the 90s that was powerful enough to encode or decode it.

↳ reply 1 — kqr:

Tangential to the tangent, but turbo codes/LDPC are algorithms for transmitting data over unreliable links with optimal redundancy for a target error rate. They underlie much of modern wireless data transfer, and were known to be possible since Shannon, but nobody had figured out how to actually do it in practise. When they were invented in the '90s everybody reacted with disbelief at first!

↳ reply 2 — jasonjayr:

Many years ago, "8088 Domination" demonstrated full motion video on the original 1981 IBM personal computer:

https://trixter.oldskool.org/2014/06/19/8088-domination-post...

As it turns out, the video was encoded in such a way that it could be played back using the display bandwidth of the original PC, BUT doing that encoding required a modern computer to perform in a reasonable amount of time.

↳ reply 3 — abetusk:

I'm having trouble finding it but there was an article a while back comparing mp3 speed gains from hardware and software. The hardware was getting better at the pace of Moore's law but the (de)compression speeds for mp3s were far outpacing it, showing that mp3 decoding optimizations were giving orders of magnitude more speedup.

I think this is a common trend for algorithms that are in wide use, where you have Moore's law like behavior on the hardware side and then also software optimizations that give their own order of magnitude speedups.

Top #2 — FartyMcFarter:

Awesome article. Nit:

> the average chess grandmaster during a classical game will analyze roughly the same number of moves as an amateur player, but they analyze only the most critical moves and do a better job with that analysis.

I don't buy this. I've seen GMs playing online while verbalizing their thought process (on twitch / youtube videos where they livestream their play), and they consider way more branches than I do, while also going deeper than I ever would on some branches. My top rating in lichess blitz is about 1900, not bad but way lower than a GM.

Ya that's definitely a simplifying lie.

It's totally true that most people overestimate how much of GM's abilities comes from pure calculation, and underrate intuition. That's what it's getting at.

But in classical games GMs are, in fact, doing tons of calculation, and the statement is literally completely false.

↳ reply 2 — aurareturn:

Human brain can do calculations in the back of their head without realizing it. Verbalizing does not mean it's all they thought about.

Top #3 — Sharlin:

> because who would want to buy a Pentium Pro when the better-in-almost-every-way Pentium MMX

Maybe this was satirizing people running after every shiny new thing, but the MMX certainly wasn’t. The Pro was the first P6, a totally new, out-of-order microarchitecture that the Pentium 2 would be based on. The MMX was a standard P5 Pentium with a larger L1 and the MMX vector instruction set which, while the first of its kind in an x86, was ultimately not used much in applications, partly because it was integer-only (also because it awkwardly co-opted the existing FPU registers rather than having its own register file). In any case, the Pros were expensive and meant for business use, while the MMXs were consumer processors.

Yes at that time Intel invented the market segmentation between "Pentium" for "consumers" and "Pentium Pro" for big spenders, and to make Pentium Pro more attractive they removed memory errors detection from the "Pentium" chipsets, which is the origin of the current state, when most non-server computers are very vulnerable to memory corruption and nobody can calculate how much money was lost by most computer owners during the last 3 decades, due to the greed of the Intel marketing, because nobody knows how many of the computer crashes or data loss cases that were typically attributed to unknown software bugs were actually caused by memory corruption.

Because this move was a money maker for all involved, all memory producers and also AMD followed immediately the Intel initiative. Memory modules without ECC would have never existed if adequate consumer protection laws had existed.

↳ reply 2 — jasonwatkinspdx:

Yeah, the Pro and MMX were totally different market segments, not alternatives for each other. The Pro's competition at the time was DEC Alpha, PA RISC, etc. It wasn't a chip that made sense for ordinary PC users at the time.

item.title: Nvidia – open-source auto-ontology
item.description: 241 points, 99 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  241 points  ·  99 comments

Top #1 — gavinray:

I want to attempt an explanation as it seems a lot of folks here didn't grok the very terribly written README

"Auto Ontology" is sort of a poor name.

Here's the problem:

Your company has data scattered across multiple types of databases. People who make decisions want to ask questions about that data.

The old way is they would go to a Data Analyst, and say, "Get me a report on so and so", and it was the Analyst's job to iron out the right series of queries and one-off scripts to generate the needed info.

With a system like this, the idea is that all your database models have been introspected and stored in a central metadata catalogue.

When a question is asked like "What were the top selling items in the month of May?", the metadata catalogue tells you "Products are stored in FOO_DB" and "Product_Sales are stored in BAR DB" and so you go and fetch the right data from the right place and do whatever in-memory calculations you need to do.

What the system provides is the implementation code for:

- Introspecting each of your DB's

- Aggregating model + metadata information in a central, virtual DB (VDB)

- Generating dialect-specific SQL from natural language queries and routing them to the right DB for the underlying table

- Combining results in-memory when a natural language query requires multiple datasources

- Handling proper permissions, etc

A GOOD system for doing this also integrates with your external API sources (OpenAPI, GraphQL, gRPC, whatever) and also documentation sources (cough, I work on this, cough).

↳ reply — throwaway5752:

"seems a lot of folks here didn't grok the very terribly written README"

I tried to make it through the README and it was just unmotivated slop. Perhaps it reads better to agents. It is like the Van Halen rider story - if the authors didn't care to write a good README, what are the odds that they paid attention to the rest of the large codebase?

↳↳ reply — Twirrim:

I ended up throwing the README at an LLM and it gave me a much simpler and clearer explanation. Copying the bits of an explanation that helped me:

> The problem it’s trying to solve is that generating valid SQL doesn’t necessarily produce the right answer. An AI might find a column called revenue, but still choose the wrong dataset or misunderstand whether that figure includes things like refunds. Auto Ontology adds information about what the data means to help it make those decisions.

and then the one paragraph summary at the end:

> My reading: it’s a database chat application built around a reusable catalogue of business meaning. The question worth testing is whether that catalogue makes answers measurably more correct—and how much human work it takes to get the definitions right.

Top #2 — grey-area:

Fixing unreliable agents by adding more unreliable agents. It's a shame we can't do something about the tendency of LLMs to give more weight to their weights than to the data they're analysing.

I guess it all comes back to the fact that they don't have a clear division between data they have learned about the world, instructions and data under analysis.

You can ask them only to consider the 5 facts in front of them, but they won't do that, and cannot do that.

↳ reply 1 — IanCal:

> Fixing unreliable agents by adding more unreliable agents.

Depending on how you combine imperfect systems, you can lower or increase error rates.

> data they have learned about the world, instructions and data under analysis.

I don't think there really is a clear distinction between these things though.

And I don't mean this in a gotcha way - these things apply to people too. Not that that means they're like people, but we have successfully built enormous systems out of fallible people, and other imperfect things.

The goal is rarely "eliminate all errors" but "have a thing that's useful, given a possibility of things going wrong".

↳↳ reply — zbentley:

> I don't think there really is a clear distinction between these things though.

Computer systems, though, can have that distinction. If you read data supplied by the user, and then process it via behavior in code, and process that result against administratively-set data in the database, the separation between user-supplied data, administratively-configured data, and instructions (code) is extremely clear. Even if you are doing something that could be nondeterministic, e.g. incorporating randomness or doing sentiment analysis or whatnot.

I don't think the oft-repeated "AI is fallible just like humans are" applies here. Computer systems are an area where that separation can be achieved. We know this because we've achieved it a lot. LLMs, powerful as they are, are a massive step back in that regard. Their benefits might outweigh that compromise, but it is, as they say, "worth naming" anyway.

↳↳↳ reply — IanCal:

> Computer systems, though, can have that distinction. If you read data supplied by the user, and then process it via behavior in code, and process that result against administratively-set data in the database, the separation between user-supplied data, administratively-configured data, and instructions (code) is extremely clear

No it is not.

They are three places you can put things, amongst an infinite other number of places you can, but they are not some inherent core distinctions.

Is a javascript file code or data? If I read it to measure file size and don't execute it, is it ever code? If I read in a file and do different things in the code based on it, and never alter that file, how is that any different from having if (x) baked into the code? Why is it user supplied data if we read in a file and do things based on the contents yet code when I read in js and execute stuff in a VM?

They are just different places with different access controls that alter the outcome. There's no magical distinction between code, data and admin data or anything else other than really who gets to change what. And then there's obviously not just three named buckets of "stuff", it's as many as you want.

> I don't think the oft-repeated "AI is fallible just like humans are" applies here.

You're missing the point here, the point is we have built big things with fallible components. Therefore the idea that a component is fallible does not just from that fact mean we can't do useful things with it. And it's a very relevant point if we're looking at "where can we use this in place of humans" - if we had a human there before we were not starting from a perfectly reliable point.

↳ reply 2 — Roark66:

Yes, also I hate the direction "frontier" is taking now. Opus 5.5 may be better in agentic coding and reverse engineering, but it has regressed greatly in instruction following.

You can give it instructions and 5k tokens later it will do exact opposite you told it to.

Top #3 — barrrrald:

I've spent a career working with data and ontologies and I couldn't understand this readme, and the diagram only makes it more confusing.

item.title: Anthropic's growth just flattened
item.description: 206 points, 240 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (regenerator1.com)

→ HN comments  ·  206 points  ·  240 comments

Top #1 — modeless:

Opus 5.5 came out right at the end of the quarter, September 22. I'm confident that it caused more usage growth since then. I'm sure there are a lot of people rooting for their IPO to fail but they are still clearly in the lead on coding and will continue to do well until someone definitively passes them.

↳ reply 1 — mdasen:

> they are still clearly in the lead on coding and will continue to do well until someone definitively passes them.

I think the first implying the second might be a bit of a stretch. At some point, companies are going to start looking at their AI spending and start negotiating deals. OpenAI is right behind them and Anthropic is around 8x more expensive (Sol 6.1 vs Opus 5.5 based on Artificial Intelligence's cost per task; cost per token is a somewhat useless metric when different models use vastly different numbers of tokens for the same thing). Chinese models like Deepseek 4.1 Flash are cheap, can be self-hosted, and while certainly behind Claude Opus 5.5, are still good.

Lots of companies buy "inferior" products like Microsoft Teams. Over the next 5 years, it seems likely that many models will get really good to the point that people often won't be able to tell any difference. Even if something isn't "definitively" better, companies might say "our engineers can't tell the difference and we're cutting our costs by 85%."

It's not absurd to think that a company would use its own harness or an open source harness and/or put a proxy in to route requests variably. For two months, they have engineers using different models unbeknownst to them and they measure things like how often the engineers have to correct or redirect the model. At the end of two months, they might find little difference in performance and switch to a much lower cost model.

It's not like it'd be crazy hard to analyze workers frustration as they did their jobs and figure out if one model was actually better. They could log all the conversations and it's not like AI can't easily determine things like "no, that's completely wrong" as a phrase showing that the agent was really off base.

I think a big part of the next 5-10 years is going to be about cost/efficiency.

↳↳ reply — Karrot_Kream:

Ultimately the question is whether there's a pareto optimal point for intelligence models. There's 2 potential worlds:

1. Frontier models are so good that the token cost of an average task becomes miniscule, so users are incentivized to use frontier models because their sheer intelligence makes them cheaper to use.

2. There is a pareto optimal point where even if you spend more on tokens overall profits decrease because token costs rise faster than revenue does.

The "no lab has a clear lead" world leads to 2.

item.title: LLMs are not superhuman at reading and writing neural network weights
item.description: 127 points, 14 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (seangoedecke.com)

→ HN comments  ·  127 points  ·  14 comments

Top #1 — nfw2:

One could say they might be "superhuman" here in the same way that LLMs might be said to be superhuman at math. Perhaps they do this work faster and more effectively than any person could manually. But they are certainly still doing it the "human" way ie reasoning with legible and coherent thoughts, rather than communing through some Matrix-like symbology which is what people who skimmed the article seem to be assuming.

↳ reply — antonvs:

That "faster and more effectively" part is undeniably superhuman, and it can result in qualitative leaps in capabilities.

For example, an LLM's ability to comprehend and explain a complex codebase, that it's never seen before, far outstrips that of any human.

People like to come up with factors to quantify how much more efficient LLMs are. A newly hired human developer working on a complex codebase can take months to get up to speed, to get a holistic understanding of how it works so that they're able to make non-trivial changes. An LLM can do it in minutes. That's a factor on the order of 10,000x.

It may not be "communing through some Matrix-like symbology," but at some point it starts to seem that way.

Top #2 — aaroninsf:

False, in a way that genuinely matters.

True: they are superhuman at every one of these tasks, in the boring way they are better—according to a wall clock and the coupled standard of actual results—at other things, just not in some mystical way.

Top #3 — lnenad:

We keep moving the goalposts, I love it. A few years ago LLMs writing simple functions was downplayed and now this. I lovehate the future this will bring.

↳ reply — aesthesia:

This isn't goalpost moving, it's pushing back against a misinterpretation of the paper's results (one that seems to have been encouraged by the authors).

↳↳ reply — lnenad:

How is it pushing back, if anything it's mostly clarifying and the conclusion aligns with the original article:

> It’s cool that Astra was able to make direct weight updates. But we shouldn’t think of this like a radically new capability that will change how AI research is done. We should think of this as analogous to the ability of LLMs to emit machine code and tweak compiled binaries: it’s an impressive trick, but the best way to work with binaries is still to write source code and compile it.

It's like people are immediately forbidden to be impressed that AI was able to do this. The original article itself mentions the mechanisms by which Astra achieved this. They just of course wanted to gain more attention so they used a sensational title, like 90% of scientists that want their stuff read.

How is it not moving goalposts, it knew how to detect which weights to update and a way to do it? Even this article says so in the part that I quoted. The original piece never stated humans are unable to do this, I don't even think it implied it. So being impressed with this accomplishment is actually *ok*.

item.title: Egoless Mathematics in the AI Era
item.description: 158 points, 113 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (terrytao.wordpress.com)

→ HN comments  ·  158 points  ·  113 comments

Top #1 — kzz102:

Human pursuits cannot be separated from the humans who pursuit it. In the pursuit of knowledge, what ultimately drives people is what they themselves can understand, and the meaning these understanding provides, both based on their own experience and people whose opinions they value. Humans do not pursuit Platonic knowledge for their own sake, and those who claim to do it, often are satisfying their egos in a different way.

↳ reply 1 — vasco:

> Humans do not pursuit Platonic knowledge for their own sake, and those who claim to do it, often are satisfying their egos in a different way.

The different way is "I'm different, my reasons are better". We are but ego.

↳ reply 2 — calf:

See, any serious Platonist would point out your line of reasoning is incoherent, because the conceit contained within such an accusation just covertly satisfies your own ego through a clever meta-discursive rhetorical maneuver. And they would be right

The truth of the matter is somewhere else and if only people were actually a bit better rounded philosophically and politically they would not be rehashing such talking points on either side of the controversy.

Top #2 — GMoromisato:

The lens to use is the Venn diagram of:

   1. What you like doing
   2. What you are good at doing
   3. What people will pay you to do
For math, if your goal is to prove something that no one else has proven, then all three are under attack.

I think the "egoless" path is taking a 50,000-foot view of mathematics that ignores the above lens. Sure, mathematics will survive and even prosper with AI, but what about the mathematicians?

In time, the profession of mathematics will evolve so a new task is at the center of the diagram--maybe it will be explaining math results to humans or teaching math to future mathematicians. I don't know. But it's easy to see that not everyone is going to be happy with the transition, and many will be left behind.

For software engineering, it depends on what your center is. If you like "writing code", then #3 is under attack. But for those whose goal is, "make something work", all three are still viable and even better than before (or at least faster).

That's why we see so much disagreement on HN about whether AI is good or bad for software engineering.

I'm sure lots of other people have made this observation before.

It is cool to see. It is better to engage than to be in denial and just fall into reactionary behavior.

item.description: 479 points, 137 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (freenode.net)

→ HN comments  ·  479 points  ·  137 comments

Top #1 — debinguy:

I find it odd that no public discussions are highlighting that iptables or nftables can drop this before the kernel CVE is exploitable by a U32 drop rule in raw PREROUTING...

sudo iptables -t raw -I PREROUTING -p tcp -m u32 ! --u32 "0>>24&0x0F=5" -j DROP

↳ reply 1 — mort96:

Does a normal "default deny all incoming" rule with e.g UFW or nftables achieve the same thing?

↳↳ reply — ranger_danger:

"default deny incoming" would apply to the filter INPUT chain, and there are several other chains that run before that one (raw, conntrack, mangle, nat), so it's better to use an explicit iptables or nft rule targeting the earliest "raw PREROUTING" chain.

Do note that eBPF can still bypass netfilter entirely, as can containers, or any process using a separate network namespace.

↳↳↳ reply — mort96:

↳ reply 2 — Lord_Zero:

I respect that there is a quick fix I can do myself with iptables. However, I don't want to have to do that. I run Ubuntu with automatic security patches enabled, I trust the Ubuntu team to issue quick fixes and my server to be patched most of the time while I am asleep. I don't want to have to manually edit my server configuration to patch security holes and have to remember all these little knobs when I get EOL and have to rebuild my server.

↳ reply 3 — ranger_danger:

I also add the same rule for OUTPUT to prevent any misbehaving apps from trying to break things.

Red Hat also claims that netfilter is not enough: https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/RHSB-2026...

> The following nftables table drops incoming IPv4 TCP packets that contain IP options, which reduces exposure to this vulnerability but cannot fully prevent it.

I know things like eBPF can technically bypass netfilter if someone tries hard enough, but I'm not sure if they're referring to any other ways to exploit this that a netfilter rule can't catch.

Firejail by default also allows unprivileged users to completely bypass any netfilter rules from the main network namespace... so if the user has that installed (even if they don't use it), it's something to keep in mind.

A system running multiple network namespaces might not have the same mitigations applied inside all of them, so be sure to check all of those, except there's no great way of even finding all the different namespaces running on a Linux system for some reason (please prove me wrong if something exists! lsns is not enough).

But yes I agree it seems strange that most posts/articles/etc. are not prominently giving out mitigation strategies.

Top #2 — c0l0:

It's rather uninteresting to note, once again, that Ubuntu has decided to do this. I would like to know the (official, if any - unofficial/speculative otherwise) reason WHY they have not.

It does not seem that complicated to patch, and kernel upgrades are a dime a dozen these days. So what is making them delay a fix for so long?

Top #3 — harry8:

Question:

Every consumer router-wirelessAP I've seen runs linux.

I never see security upgrades for the kernels they use. Not one. Not ever.

Is this something that should be a cause for concern? Even if you don't run a consumer-grade tplink, netgear, asus, whatever router yourself.

Update: The context which I should have said is that I think LLMs are giving script kids nation state level tools and expertise. This known bug is always less interesting than the next twenty.

↳ reply 1 — LaurensBER:

Is it a cause of concern? Yes. Will you get hacked? Most likely not.

Most consumer routers run ancient stacks with all kinds of weird proprietary vendor patches that are tied to a specific kernel version. Looking at you Qualcomm!

However they generally also drop all traffic by default so from the WAN side they look like a black hole. I guess that's "safe" enough for most consumers.

For fun, take a look at the open PRs in the OpenWRT repos. Those people are doing some amazing work but it's also frustrating to see them struggle with things that _could_ be easy if the vendor made some slightly better choices.

I would strongly prefer something like OpenWRT though. Call me paranoid but after the last few weeks I'm increasingly less comfortable with connecting my devices to a blackbox.

↳↳ reply — j45:

It's a massive risk, and only a matter of time. Especially for hardware that's no longer updated firmware wise.

I'm thinking of what to do myself.

The ghost of android releasing 6 month old patches every month is going to come home to roost.

↳ reply 2 — estebarb:

Mosty probably: not. Traffic passes throught the ASIC, usually it is not processed on CPU or custom code. Unlike typical web servers, that reduces the attack surface as there aren't software parsers (a common place where vulnerabilities hide). Additionally the OS may have additional protection measures, such as signing each binary, signing the booting image and limiting which syscalls can be done by any binary.

item.title: Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen
item.description: 2538 points, 784 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (rikiyat.github.io)

→ HN comments  ·  2538 points  ·  784 comments

Top #1 — vessenes:

This is insane.

Astra can, without tooling, determine what games small networks are trained on, can edit the weights of networks directly to improve outcomes, and can hand edit a small qwen model to improve its math skills by like 5x.

I'm shook. If you'd asked me this morning whether LLMs have native understanding of their weights that is less than human <-> neuron understanding, the same as human or more than human, I would have said "same to less" depending on definitions.

No human can go edit a brain to become better at math. This is just very, very surprising to me and extremely interesting. I would guess this upsets quite a number of interp theories and philosophical takes on what's going on with these networks.

↳ reply 1 — l9o:

I think the "taught qwen math" part is not exactly correct though, even if the post makes it sound like that. Qwen already knew math, but it was bugging out and getting into an infinite loop when it tried to solve the problems (85 of its first 96 answers hit the token limit). With numpy and pytorch, Astra found where the loop was happening and fixed it.

They also tried the same with Gemma 3 270M, which doesn't loop and is just bad at math, and Astra couldn't improve it. Still impressive, but it's more in the realm of what I'd expect, given labs are probably training their models on ML research and interpretability work.

↳↳ reply — ch_sm:

I agree, this is important context. They call it out explicitly. However, even identifying clusters that specialize in certain fields automatically and then finding and fixing learning “errors” is incredibly impressive to me. Especially for medium sized local models between 20B an 70B parameters, this could yield huge capability and efficiency improvements, not to speak of the potentially enormous downstream effects that come with interpretability.

↳ reply 2 — Aurornis:

LLMs have been used to investigate and improve LLMs for a long time. Drawing parallels to human brains and neurons isn't all that interesting other than as a philosophical abstraction.

The work done in this experiment could have also been done by a sufficiently motivated human with enough time to explore, though obviously we would need more tools to visualize and track things. There have been a lot of interesting LLM introspection tools that allow you to peek into the model and see what's being activated and run experiments to trigger it.

Are you familiar with abliterated or "uncensored" models where weights have been modified to avoid triggering refusal patterns? You take an LLM, create test cases that trigger the refusal pattern, observe weights involved in that response, then tweak those weights until the response is reduced. This is the same type of work, applied to a specific type of error that was impeding math within Qwen. That work can also be done with an LLM in a harness running the experiments. The amazing part here is that Astra was large enough to walk through the problem without other tooling doing it experimentally.

So I don't think your analogy of a human modifying a neuron is quite applicable. LLM weights are not neurons and they've been inspectable, by humans or LLMs in a harness, for a long time.

↳ reply 3 — mentos:

I’m just a layman but this feels like a big discovery on par with attention is all you need. For an LLM to have such incredible intuition of weights feels very emergent and unanticipated?

Top #2 — xg15:

And here we go...

As others have said, while still absolutely insane, I don't find it completely out-of-the-blue surprising. One of the recurring abilities of (current-generation) LLMs seem to be to rapidly grasp very complex systems, where humans would need months or years to reach the same level of expertise.

You can see this in the way a coding agent can "understand" and explain sprawling legacy codebases in seconds.

You can also see it in the projects that are using them to reverse-engineer proprietary IoT protocols or computer games.

But those were all systems where we had detailed knowledge about what structures are there to be reverse-enginered.

If the models can transfer this ability to some other systems where we don't know the underlying structure then I think we will be in for a lot more craziness in the future. (Protein interaction networks? DNA sequences? Ecosystem interactions? Animal languages?)

As for weights, if the models really can analyze the semantics behind specific weights or directions, I have my hopes that they could also give a textual explanation or help designing tools to make "handcrafting" weights more practical in general.

↳ reply 1 — Nevermark:

The way I interpete it, is vast amounts of text are to LLMs, in some ways like vision is to us. Not seeing tokens, but seeing the "shapes" between them. Like we don't parse pixels but see the whole picture at once.

They triangulate efficiently on the meaning from all the text, instead of rolling it through a lossy feedback system.

It is why they are so good at processing ambiguity. They can combine ambiguity from any parts of the text, near equally well, even on long form text.

Just like we can instantly triangulate the meaning out of barely lit photographs, by correlating every little shadow or bit of texture, regardless of where the clues are in the image.

↳ reply 2 — suriyaG:

but code is made to be understandable. while neural nets are not.

that is why this is crazy,

give a human a legacy codebase and 5 years and he'll be able to understand very well.

if you give a human the weights of qwen 0.8B and 5 years it'll still be impossible to edit the weights in any legible manner.

Top #3 — vanyle:

I don't think this is an emergent capability. I think Astra was trained on neural weights data as an attempt by OpenAI to get to recursive self improvement.

Something similar happen in early GPT models which had a lot of chess game in standard notation in their training data which made them very good at chess as long as your prompt had the right format.

We'll see if this attempt at RSI worked.

↳ reply 1 — elanning:

> I think Astra was trained on neural weights data as an attempt by OpenAI to get to recursive self improvement.

This might be the case, a few weeks ago, I wanted to compare a small neural network trained with AdamW vs a handcrafted set of weights on a random task. Astra was able to handcraft a set of weights that perfectly fit the small neural network to the task. AdamW was unable to tune the weights to get the same result.

I believe we've known humans can handcraft weights much more efficiently than standard gradient descent methods, we just don't have enough memory or time to scale ourselves, so it makes sense to train a neural network to do it on our behalf. I am excited to see how far we can push this method.

Mentioned chat: https://chatgpt.com/share/6ae8f024-34ec-83e8-9572-1300f52c80...

↳↳ reply — kragen:

It looks like Astra picked the "random task", and the task it picked was 8-bit parity, which is easy to design a circuit for that computes the answer perfectly, but sort of maximally difficult to fit with any kind of gradient descent. It's a great choice for what you asked, which was to find a case where AdamW doesn't come close to the theoretical optimum fit. But I'm less convinced that it tells us much about Astra's capabilities at handcrafting weights in general.

8-bit parity is a^b^c^d^e^f^g^h, which you can compute with minimal depth as ((a^b)^(c^d))^((e^f)^(g^h)). You can compute x^y as x&~y | y&~x. With ReLU activation, i | j is ReLU(i + j): weights of 1, bias of 0. And i & ~j is ReLU(i - j): weights of 1 and -1, still bias of 0. So a two-input XOR is three neurons in two layers, and the tree of 7 binary XORs is 21 neurons in 6 hidden layers. I don't know why Astra needed 433 parameters. Only 42 nonzero parameters are needed. Maybe the other 391 parameters are zeros that the Transformer model demands to be present.

With an RNN you can compute the parity of a string of any length with only three neurons.

Actually, I handed that to Claude Opus 5.5 to check, and it sensibly pointed out that x&~y is mutually exclusive with y&~x, so XOR doesn't even need the third neuron, except in the last layer; you can just fold the addition into the weights of the next layer, which means you only need 4 layers and 15 neurons. But about half of those neurons need 4 nonzero input weights instead of 2, so you still need 42 nonzero weights. It's a good thing you don't need those OR neurons, too, because my definition is wrong: ReLU(1+1) = 2.

Also it explained how to design a 28-parameter net that I don't quite understand, and also a single-hidden-layer network with 8 ReLUs, which I also don't understand, but it needs more parameters: $\text{parity}=s+\sum_{k=1}^{7}2(-1)^k\,\mathrm{ReLU}(s-k)$ where I think $s=\sum_i x_i$.

Somewhat more surprisingly, it also said it didn't have any trouble fitting a 641-parameter network to this problem with AdamW.

↳↳↳ reply — kragen:

Here is the code Opus 5.5 is claiming fits a 641-parameter MLP to parity of 8 inputs:

  # Fits small MLPs to 8-bit parity (the full 256-row truth table) with
  # full-batch AdamW, written out in numpy (no PyTorch, so it won't match a
  # PyTorch run bit for bit), and reports for each shape how many of 20 seeds
  # reach 100% accuracy and the median accuracy. Needs Python 3.9+ and numpy.
  import itertools

  import numpy as np

  X = np.array(list(itertools.product([0, 1], repeat=8)), float)  # all 256 inputs
  y = X.sum(1) % 2


  def nparams(widths: list[int]) -> int:
      """Parameter count of a dense MLP with these layer widths, biases included."""
      return sum(a * b + b for a, b in zip(widths, widths[1:]))


  def train(
      widths: list[int],
      seed: int,
      steps: int = 4000,
      lr: float = 1e-2,
      wd: float = 1e-4,
  ) -> float:
      """Full-batch AdamW on all 256 inputs; returns the final training accuracy."""
      rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
      P = []    # parameters: W0, b0, W1, b1, ...
      for a, b in zip(widths, widths[1:]):
          bound = 1 / np.sqrt(a)    # same as PyTorch nn.Linear's default init
          P += [rng.uniform(-bound, bound, (a, b)), rng.uniform(-bound, bound, b)]

      m = [np.zeros_like(p) for p in P]    # Adam first moments
      v = [np.zeros_like(p) for p in P]    # Adam second moments
      nlayers = len(widths) - 1
      for step in range(1, steps + 1):
          hs = [X]    # hs[i] is the input to layer i
          zs = []     # pre-activations
          h = X
          for i in range(nlayers):
              z = h @ P[2 * i] + P[2 * i + 1]
              zs.append(z)
              h = np.maximum(z, 0) if i < nlayers - 1 else z    # ReLU; linear output
              hs.append(h)

          logit = h[:, 0]
          prob = 0.5 * (1 + np.tanh(logit / 2))    # sigmoid without overflow
          g = ((prob - y) / len(y))[:, None]    # d(mean cross-entropy)/d(logit)
          G = [None] * len(P)    # gradients, parallel to P
          for i in reversed(range(nlayers)):
              G[2 * i] = hs[i].T @ g
              G[2 * i + 1] = g.sum(0)
              if i > 0:
                  g = (g @ P[2 * i].T) * (zs[i - 1] > 0)

          # AdamW, using PyTorch's default values for betas (0.9, 0.999) and eps (1e-8)
          for k in range(len(P)):
              P[k] -= lr * wd * P[k]    # decoupled weight decay
              m[k] = 0.9 * m[k] + 0.1 * G[k]
              v[k] = 0.999 * v[k] + 0.001 * G[k] ** 2
              P[k] -= lr * (m[k] / (1 - 0.9 ** step)) / (
                  np.sqrt(v[k] / (1 - 0.999 ** step)) + 1e-8)

      # accuracy of the last forward pass, i.e. before the final update
      return ((logit > 0) == (y > 0.5)).mean()


  for w in [[8, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1], [8, 8, 4, 2, 1], [8, 8, 1], [8, 16, 1], [8, 64, 1]]:
      accs = [train(w, seed) for seed in range(20)]
      print(w, nparams(w), "params; seeds at 100%:", sum(a == 1 for a in accs),
            "/ 20; median acc", np.median(accs))
I might not know enough about ANNs to spot if it's cheating on some way, but it looks legit. It does indeed output that the [8, 64, 1] configuration gets 100% accuracy on all 20 seeds.

↳ reply 2 — krona:

All NN behaviour is emergent strictly speaking; by definition. I think you mean a phase shift of a kind; a qualitative, unpredictable leap in capability.

Top #1 — olyjohn:

Speaking of getting into Microsoft events, some buddies and I registered with Microsoft as OEM system builders when we were in high school. We would drive to Redmond and attend these events talking about various new hardware and software and would leave with bags full of swag and they had awesome Raffles giving away some expensive shiny new hardware, which we would win quite often shockingly.

We had finally heard about the Microsoft store on campus, and had heard about the super discounted software. Turned out you had to be an employee. We were crushed because retail copies of Win2k were expensive for high schoolers. So we sat out in front of the store with signs "will work for cheap Microsoft software." Finally this girl came by and asked what we were doing, she was an intern or a new hire or something like that not much older than us, still in college. She went into to store and came out with boxed copies of Win2k Workstation for $20 a pop for us. We were stoked and tried to give he some cash, but she was just happy to help us out.

Those were some good times. I wonder if stuff like that still happens today.

↳ reply — kmoser:

My story of getting into a Microsoft event: in late 2000, Microsoft was rebranding MSN with the butterfly logo and they paid groups of inline skaters in NYC to dress up in custom purple velour body suits with wings to skate around Manhattan and generate buzz (heh) about the new MSN.

Well, there happened to be a computer show at the Javits Center so we skated there, convinced a security guard we were with Microsoft (hey, eight skaters in velour MSN body suits must be with Microsoft, right?), and skated onto the show floor. About fifteen minutes later security figured out we weren't part of the show and kicked us out. (We weren't supposed to keep the butterfly outfits but some people did. I didn't keep mine, but I do have photos that prove it really happened.)

Top #1 — CobrastanJorji:

> Will it rain over forty percent of the city? Will it rain for forty percent of the day? Or does the speaker just not know and is too shy to say so?

Unrelated, but to answer his question, it's the probability that a random spot in the covered area will get at least a smidge of rain at some point in the covered time period. A 10% chance of rain can mean either that the forecaster is 100% sure that exactly 10% of the area will get rain, or it can mean that the forecaster sees a large rainstorm nearby which would cover the whole area if it arrived, but which only has a 10% chance of arriving. Or anything in between. If there's a rain cloud meandering over the city, covering 1% of the city at a time, and over the whole day it randomly walks over 10% of the city, that's also a 10% chance.

↳ reply — noduerme:

I had wondered about this. What you're saying makes sense, but, living in Portland, I had come up with my own explanation. When I see 10% here, I usually take it to mean something like "it will rain for six minutes every hour", or for 10% of the day.

item.title: Polyend releases the Tracker firmware source code
item.description: 127 points, 39 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (polyend.com)

→ HN comments  ·  127 points  ·  39 comments

Top #1 — consumer451:

This has to be related to MWAVE's FM-1 viral popularity, largely due to open firmware right?

https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/10/from-impulse-purchas...

https://github.com/aroum/fm1-custom-fw

see also:

> Reverse Engineering of the M-VAVE FM-1 Pocket Synthesizer Firmware

https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49994065 (75 points - 50 comments)

↳ reply 1 — vvillena:

That, plus the fact people were already poking into the closed firmware binary, plus the existence of an alternative firmware. By doing this, Polyend also kind of passes the responsibility of maintaining the Tracker devices to the community.

It's also worth mentioning that the release is not just a source code release, they added a lot of great features like sample streaming, and dedicated velocity and timing lanes. And they released APIs so that people can easily create new synth engines and effects.

↳↳ reply — mycall:

Bring Roland VSynth capabilities to it.

↳ reply 2 — rickdeckard:

It's more likely because LLM usage and particularly REA (Reverse Engineer Anything) is opening up those firmwares whether the vendor likes it or not.

The best strategy for a HW-vendor at this point is to get ahead of it and open-source the firmware under your own License Agreement, so you can possibly also integrate community work back into your official firmware.

I'm happy that some move in this direction.

The much more terrible strategy is litigation and moving as much logic as possible away from the product into some cloud-service (requiring periodic online-connection, etc.).

We already see both trajectories, so I hope the customers will decide wisely which strategy to fund...

↳ reply 3 — anigbrowl:

Yes. Custom firmware for audio gear has been A Thing for a long time, as far back as the 1990s. I worked on a company that offered a general DSP platform back in 2003, but it didn't take off because it was too difficult for most people to program. JJOS became very popular among users of Akai's MPC line (of whom there are very many) in the mid-2000s.

The combinations of LLMs and agentic reverse-engineering skills have sent things into overdrive in recent months. As well as allowing people to repurpose cheap gear like the M-VAVE it has also revealed that a lot of larger vendors have been outright lying to their users about hardware limitations to more effectively segment their target market. In my the future is high quality controllers/converters with a generic SOC inside. Behringer is already going down this route and has the manufacturing heft to do it quickly and with a decent level of quality. Akai also seems to have jumped in on the trend.

Top #2 — sebastienbarre:

For people afraid of bricking their units, I can't stress enough how groundbreaking it is that they're acknowledging that risk and still offering to repair your unit. You pay of course, because this is a risk you took, but at least they will have a look at it:

    "Out-of-Warranty Repairs Available: In the unlikely event that something ever goes wrong with your hardware while using custom firmware, it is not covered under standard warranty. However, Polyend is always happy to help get your instrument back up and running through its official out-of-warranty repair service (standard service, parts, and shipping fees apply."

↳ reply — mycall:

Does the board come with a jtag interface to unbrick the device?

Top #3 — dimatura:

The avalanche of reverse engineered/custom firmwares is definitely changing the synth landscape. I'm wondering how many other companies will start open sourcing. It isn't always trivial since sometimes there's proprietary software components or toolchains that can't be open sourced. But it's hard to imagine it won't be more common. There's a lot of mixed feelings in the community. A lot of musicians don't like AI, but they do want to have more features and bug fixes. A lot of synth makers are probably ambivalent too, especially if they have a stronger vision of what the synths should be that custom firmware ignore. Not to mention the commercial implications of adding features into existing synths, possibly making newer models less appealing. And of course people are copying UIs and workflows from other synths that took a lot of work to develop.

Which would be another really cool demo.

Super cool. You're going to be working 80 hour weeks for the next year, I'm excited to see what you put out!
